stand that they wish to construct and operate railways, tramways, telephone and telegraph lines in Brazil, subject to the laws of that country. Mr. Speaker, representing as I do, one of the ridings in which crude petroleum is produced and in which an independent Canadian refinery is situated, and believing as I do, that the production of crude oil and the refining of same, forms one of the most important industries in our Dominion. X am anxious to give to the House all the information I can, hoping that this government may see the justice of my plea, and that they will abandon the resolution with reference to oil, which is now before the House.
I realize my utter inability to do justice to this industry in attempting to defend it. I also feel that an irreparable wrong will be done this industry if this resolution is adopted. At the outset, let me state that with reference to this industry I am purely and simply a producer. X have not a dollar in a refinery, or a by-product manufacture. I cannot believe, that the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) was conversant with the facts, needs, and requirements of this industry, when, on the 7th of this month, he placed on the table of this House, a resolution, which, if allowed to carry, will blast and blight our business for all time to come.
The hon. the Finance Minister was right when he stated, that no item in the tariff had received more attention in past years, than had the duty on oil since 1868. The Act which refers to crude oil, and its byproducts, has been amended eleven times. Several of which amendments were not very important, while others were of vital importance to our industry. In 1868 there
was an excise tax of five cents per gallon being paid to the revenue of this country. In 1877 that tax was taken off. Some years later a tax was placed on oil, and since that time it has been howled at, the tariff tinkered and tampered with, and now, before the present government leave office they give it a parting kick. If this were all, the industry might not have so much to complain of, but when you find members of parliament, backed, I am sorry to say, by many of the newspapers of our country, making a football of this industry, not only on the floor of this House, but on the platforms through our country, making the most reckless, unfair, and untrue statements. With reference to our business the wonder to me is that the industry is alive to-day.
And, Mr. Speaker, were it not for the unfailing, dogged, determined pluck of our people and the confidence they have that there is plenty of oil to be found in Canada, if only capital could be induced to take hold of the business ; were it not also that ten million dollars have been invested in this industry by men, most of whom know no other business, the Canadian oil industry would not now be in existence. No other business could be kicked from pillar to post, discouraged at every turn, cut and slashed at from one end of this Dominion to the other by men who have not the first conception of the necessities of that industry, and still live. The cry of the oil people is : Will the time ever come when a definite policy with regard to the oil tariff can be assured Lo them for any number of years ? Our industry is largely a speculative industry, and we all know that it takes little to discourage capital and divert it from an enterprise of such a nature. Were it not for the constant agitation carried on in this country and the frequent tinkering with the oil tariff, there is not a doubt in my mind that to-day we would not only be supplying the home market, but we would be exporting large quantities of oil. In order to show how, with reference to our industry, great quantities of oil can be produced out of a very small area of land, I wish to call the attention of the House to a few statements in the * Oil Investors' Journal,' with reference to the Texas field, and what result the Texas field will have on our market I will not venture to assert. For instance, in the year 1902 the Beaumont field in Texas produced from about 200 acres of land, some 17,000,000 barrels of oil ; in 1903, the Sour Lake field, from about 200 acres of land, produced 7,000,000 barrels of oil ; the Batson field, from a little over 200 acres, has within three mouths produced over 4,000,000 barrels of oil. And when I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that oil in Beaumont was selling in the year 1902 for two and three cents a barrel, you can readily see that there is a possibility of Texas oil being a factor in our market.

Mr. 1IEYD. Did you say it was sold for three cents a barrel ?

Yes, Sir ; and I will read from the ' Oil Investors' Journal ' to satisfy you as to that:
Mr. Oliphant's figures at best are approximate, and he is correct in valuing the oil at what it brought the producers. Spindletop oil sold as low at 2 and 3 cents early in 1902, such prices being the inevitable outcome of the subdivision of the hill into very small tracts of land, which were sold at enormous prices -$3,500 for a thirty-second of an acre being the average figure, although instances are on record where a twenty-fourth of an acre brought $12,000.
What is the nature of the Texas oil as compared with our oil ?
The gravity of the oil in the Batson field is stated here.

The Batson field is within twenty or thirty miles of the Beaumont.

Value of Batson Oil for Refining.

I would like for my own information, to know what the gravity of the oil was that was selling at two or three cents per barrel, and which the hon. gentleman thought might come into competition with our oil.

I have not the information with me, but I may say with reference to the Beaumont and Sour Lake fields that the gravity is not as high as it is in the Batson field, which has lately come into existence. Now, Sir, let me point out what they have accomplished in that field within three years. Six refineries have been built in Beaumont and Port Arthur, and they are shipping their product to the nortli. Between the 1st of January and the 28th of April they shipped out of Port Arthur 3,116,242 barrels, which will give you some idea of the extent to which the oil is expbrted from that field. Dozens of Standard Oil Mr. ARMSTRONG.
tank steamers are bringing that oil to Philadelphia, New York and the northern states. Now, Sir, previous to the present agitation in this country, which was brought about by the standard Oil Company to serve their own selfish ends, every one of the seventy drilling rigs owned by the people of Petrolea, and in connection with which over 200 men are employed, were distributed throughout the length and breadth of our Dominion searching night and day for crude oil and gas. But, Sir, for several weeks pash if you were to go to Petrolea you would find numbers of drillers walking our streets, the rigs shut down, the development at a standstill, and confidence in the future of our industry shaken as it never was before. And, why, Mr. Speaker ? It is because the government of this country have been dickering with the Standard Oil Company and with the tariff, and they have placed the producer, the independent refiner and the consumer entirely in the hands of the Standard Oil Company.
About six years ago the Standard Oil Company purchased a small refinery in the town of Petrolia, and before one year had elapsed four other refineries in our town had been purchased by them, thus giving them the control of the refining industry in Canada at that time. The Standard Oil Company then purchased a large block of land in the town of Sarnia, they tore down the Petrolea refineries, making use of such of the materials as they could in building their plant at Sarnia ; they then built a plant larger than was necessary for the refining of our product and commenced to take control of our market. About four years ago the Standard Oil Company refused to supply the gas companies of Canada with the product used to assist in the manufacture of gas. In consequence of that the gas men came to the government asking for free oil. This request was refused by the government. Representatives of the gas companies came to Petrolea and contracted with the independent producers, many of whom have been supplying gas companies up to the present time. When the Standard Oil Company found the gas men were obtaining the crude oil for manufacturing, word came from New York-from which centre we must expect to receive all future orders-to supply the gas companies with oil, and consequently the Standard Oil Company commenced at once to squeeze the Canadian producers out of competition, and they have been successful.
In what way did they squeeze out the producers ?
By the action of this government, Sir.
But you have not told us how.
They have absolute control of the market; not a doubt about it.
That does not answer my question. How could they squeeze out the producer, except by lowering the price ?
Have not the trusts and monopolies squeezed out the binder twine and barbed wire factories ?
You have not explained that yet.
Order.
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of importance, and I do not want to ask the hon. gentleman a question unless he is willing.
Tell us about cutlery.

Never mind the cutlery ; we are not discussing that now. The hon. gentleman says the Standard Oil Company squeezed out the producers and I want to know how they could do it except by reducing the price of crude oil ?

If you listen to what I have to say, you will find out before I get througn how they do it. The petroleum Act was amended on the 29th of June, 1897, by this government, granting to the Standard Oil Trust the importation of oil in tank ships. I want you to notice the step by step taken by the Standard Oil Company, leading up to the 7th inst. See how well laid their plans were, and how successfully they have been carried out. By tank ships, many of which they own, the crude oil can be brought from Toledo, Ohio, to Sarnia, where the Standard Oil Company's refinery is situated, at a very small cost.
About two years ago, a number of producers, being dissatisfied with the treatment they were receiving at the hands of the Standard Oil Company, purchased land and built a refinery in Petrolea. which has been extended, and employs 65 men and cost $250,000. This company has been most successful in competing with the Standard, and within the past few months, have secured independent distributing stations, situated In the principal cities and towns, in the Dominion. It has over 300 stockholders, many of whom are among our brightest and best business men, and all but one or two I understand are Canadians. But then. Mr. Speaker, this government does not believe in uanada for the Canadians. It is Canada for the binder twine trust, the Standard Oil Trust, and any other trust that will pay the price.
Well, about one year ago, the Standard Oil Company stated to some of our prominent producers, that unless the tariff on crude oil was reduced to such an extent that they could import, manufacture, and distribute its products throughout our country at a profit, they, the Standard Oil Trust, would be compelled to agitate among the members of parliament, and the Ministers of the Crown, and on the platforms and in the press throughout our country, until they received what they wanted. Naturally our people felt that they should at least investigate the matter. A meeting of the producers was called ; explanations were made to our people, that unless the duty on crude oil was reduced to where the Standard Oil Company wanted it, they would at once, apply to parliament. A committee of 25 producers was appointed, to meet with the representatives of the two refineries, to hear their grievances. The committee was called; the Standard representatives refused to treat with so large a committee, whereupon the committee was reduced to nine. The nine men met the representatives of both refineries, and, after discussing the question for several days, refused to accept the Standard's proposition. The Standard men then came to Ottawa, and were refused their request, which was, to leave the duty on refined, at 5 cents per gallon, but reduce the duty on crude to 2 cents per gallon.
Why the government of this country would refuse any concessions last year, and this year grant more than any desire the Standard Oil Company ever made public, is one of the Chinese puzzles of the present session. The Standard Oil Company were prepared, up to two months ago, to pay for all crude oil coming into this country, a tariff of 2 cents per gallon. If the refined oil will be all made in Canada, as we are assured it will, now that the crude can come in free, what matter if the tariff be 2J cents or 5 cents if the Standard have control of our market ? It is estimated that it will take
1.000.	000 barrels of crude, to refine sufficient oil to supply this country for one year.
1.000.	000 barrels of crude oil at 2 cents duty per gallon, would amount to $700,000. This is a dead loss to the country, and a clear gain to the Standard Oil Company, because they would have paid that and had control of the market. Now they have the same control of the market, and don't have to pay a cent for it. However the government refused the Standard Oil Company control of our markets last year. The Standard men went home, and in a few months they started the agitation again among the producers. After months of manipulating with the producers and the government of this country, they finally obtained signatures from about 100 producers, many of whom -were in their employ and others situated near Standard pipe lines, through which their oil had to be shipped, while a large number signed it through fear. This petition was brought to the government a few months ago. I have a copy of it here, and I will recite a few clauses, so as to give you the nature of the petition :
Therefore while we strongly assert that any reduction in the present tariff upon the refined products of petroleum would be disastrous to our mining industry, and injurious in many ways. And we inseparably connect this assertion with our further statement, when we say that for the purpose of increasing

the manufacture of refined oils in Canada, we assent to the reduction of the present tariff upon crude oil of 5 cents, and 2j cents per gallon for all purposes.
The Governor in Council retaining or acquiring the power to make all regulations regarding the importation of such oil.
There was another petition presented at the meeting held in the town hall, Sarnia, at which the Standard representatives were present. That petition was largely signed by the citizens of Sarnia, from a purely selfish motive. Though not owning an oil well, they, from purely selfish motives, thought that a few more men would be employed in Sarnia if the crude oil was brought in ; and they were assisted in the matter by the hon. member for West Lamb-ton (Mr. Johnston), who, I believe, has received several telegrams of congratulations from the Standard Oil Company, New York, and their supporters. I cannot help thinking that the hundreds of farmers in his back townships will have a different story to tell. I will read a paragraph or two from that petition, which will show the generosity of the people of that town, towards our industry :
That the reduction of the duty on crude to 2 cents, while maintaining the duty of 5 cents on refined, would not in the opinion of your petitioners result in the loss of any revenue of this Dominion.
That in view of these facts, your petitioners would humbly request that the duty on crude oil be reduced to 2 cents per gallon and that the duty on refined oil be maintained at 5 cents per gallon as at present.
Brave patriotic people of Sarnia 1 Do they not realize that by their action and this government's action, the Canadian oil industry is vitally injured, and drillers and workmen are left to eke out an existence as best they can ?
The independent producers, circulated a petition, and it is to-day in the hands of the government, with some 400 names on it, asking that no action be taken. Many towns and townships in Western Ontario, presented petitions, asking that no action be taken. I believe the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) received a petition from his own town demanding that no reduction be made on the duty on oil.
What do you mean by a petition from my town ?
A resolution passed by your board of trade.
Yes.

The representatives of the Standard Oil Company have been here and in Montreal, the latter place being very easy to reach for a quiet talk. The representatives of the producers, and the independent refiners have been here, but the Standard Oil Company won. and the people all over this country are asking to-day

I was referring to the fact that the government of this country are against us and also the Standard Oil Company, and I am sorry to say that in many eases the press to some extent is against us. X am glad to say that previous to the government taking action, many of the prominent newspapers were strongly opposed to any reduction in the duty on oil. I have here a book of clippings from many newspapers with reference to the oil industry and many of these are of a most condemnatory character of the policy of the government.
What guarantee has the producer that this is the last slash he is going to have ? How do we know that before the year is out something else may drop. I would like to ask the Finance Minister why has this industry been singled out for special attack, at this time ? Why did 'the government not wait until their commission was appointed before dealing with the matter.
The oil men court investigation, they invite inspection of their industry, but they condemn any action being taken without a fair trial.
The oil industry of the Dominion has been neglected and ignored by the government. Previous to their coming to power, a few thousands of dollars were spent each year in development for gas and oil, which was of great use to men looking for a new oil and gas field.
Since 1898 not one dollar has been spent in development, and the mining reports show that thousands of dollars worth of tools and drilling material is stored at Edmonton, rusting and rotting, while the industry is being sold to the Standard Oil Company.
The government of this country, both in the reports of the provincial House and the Geological reports of this House, seem to try and take as little notice of our industry as they can possibly do.

Take the report of the Bureau of Mines of Ontario ; it takes up 43 pages of that report talking about the peat industry. While the oil industry, in which more money for development is spent in one day by private individuals than is spent in a whole year in developing the peat industry, less than three pages is given, and the log of one well; yet there has not been less than 500 wells drilled in all parts of Ontario during that time. Never in our history have drills been so successfully worked or at least, so continually at work throughout the length and breadth of our Dominion as within the past two years. In the Geological Department here even a worse state of things exists. The last report devoted to the gas and petroleum industry of our country is dated 1891. The report of the Bureau of Mines devotes a few pages to statistics, and gives the log of a few wells, but not a general summary of the work.
1 have had occasion to spend a great deal of time in the Geological Department, and I find a most deplorable state of affairs. Here is Dr. Bell, a man who has done more for the development of the mines and resources of this country than any man living. A man who has devoted a life-time to his country, being 48 years in the civil service, appointed as acting director, which office he has held for going on four years, am I not justified in asking why this man is not gazetted ? He is a man, who has been responsible, more than any other man, for the development of our resources, a man eminently qualified to fill the position. A man to whom the people of this country are indebted for the greater part of the topography of this Dominion. A man whose ability cannot be questioned, whose writings and works are of the greatest interest to our people and to the civilized world.
Dr. Bell is one of the best scientific men of this age, his explorations and writings are invaluable to our country. He is a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, the Geographical Societies of London and America, the Chemical Society of London, and of the Royal Society of London. The last mentioned distinction is considered the culmination of the ambition of British scientists and last year King Edward conferred on him the Companionship of the Imperial Service Order ' for faithful service.' He is a perfect storehouse of information about Canada, and I hope the Minister of the Interior will not let another week go by without gazetting him. Dr. Bell is merely holding his office from day to day, and cannot be expected to initiate new regulations, hence he cannot do justice to his department or to the country.
It is not the fault of the civil servants of the Geological Department that more information is not furnished with reference to the oil industry, it is the fault of the Minister of the Interior. Tens of thousands 154
of dollars are spent each year in prospecting and developing the mines of this country, and the oil business is taken little notice of. $123,930 was spent in the Geological Department in 1903 and only a little mite of this has been spent in furnishing information about gas or oil. $152,666.25 is to be voted this year being an increase of $28,736.25. I wonder how much the Minister of the Interior can spare for oil and gas development.
While I am at the question, I would like to call the Minister of the Interior's attention to what I believe a most serious blunder in his management of the Geological Department.
"When I first came here I had occasion to obtain a number of reports of the Geological Department and was compelled to pay for same. On inquiry I found that the department had a man whose sole duty was to collect the money for these reports,, and that his salary amounted to more than the money collected. Another instance of this business''government. Tons of these reports are in the cellar moulding and rotting. Surely if this government can spend from $123,000 to $153,000 each year in obtaining information, a few hundred dollars would be well spent in distributing it. What is the sense of sending men through this land gathering informaltiorp and then bottling it up and keeping a man to collect 10, 15, 20, or 25 cents on these volumes, when he does not collect enough to cover the salary he is paid. Surely the Minister of the Interior will remedy this state of things, and first of all place Dr. Bell where he ought to be.
Part of this matter may appear a little off my subject, but it all has a distinct bearing on the oil question because we have been neglected at every turn.
Remember this, that every barrel of crude that comes into our country, brings with it all the by-products, all the benzine, gasolene, naphtha, tar, coke, fuel oil, lubricating oils of all kinds from that used on the bycicle and sewing machine to the grade used on the railroad engines, besides paraffine wax, paraffine candles, vaseline, and most of the ' ines ' in the drug store, chewing gum, hair oil, all of which are taken from the crude oil. Who do you suppose will control the market for all these by-products ? Is it the man who will manufacture them ? No. You will find the Standard Oil making the first price. Why? Simply because the crude comes in free, and brings in all these by-products with it, and the Standard is, and will be, the only refinery that will handle the American crude. How much will the farmer and the workingman get out of these things ? When the farmer goes to buy lubricating oil for his machinery, will he be able to get it for less ? Will he be able to buy his machinery for less because the manufacturers get the fuel oil in free ?



Will the workman buy his tools at any lower price ? Will his benzine to mix paints be cheaper ? Will the man with his gasolene and naphtha launch or his automobile obtain any benefit through these [DOT]articles being on the free list ? I fear not. It may be like the Grand Trunk Pacific-[DOT] start off with a great blowing of trumpets, -offering great things to this Dominion, and then, within one short year, fall with a thud, leaving hon. gentlemen opposite sorry for ever having launched shell a wildcat scheme. So, to-day, the Standard reduce the price of refined and raise the price of crude as a sop to the people for what they have accomplished. It is strange how soon the managers of the Standard in the distributing stations jump into print to assure the people that no one is hurt. They have given a regular pyrotechnic display-the Minister of Finance objected to my using the expression ' fireworks,' so I had to hunt up another word. They have been making that display, and, no doubt the government of this country have made arrangements with them practically for that display. Certainly, this is small politics. But rumour has it that the Finance Minister did not prepare this resolution, that it is the production of the hon. member foi London (Mr. Hyman), who has, without previous knowledge, given out the word that he was thoroughly acquainted with the oil business and knew the condition exactly. Mr. Speaker, I stake my reputation on the assertion that neither of these men prepared the resolution, and that they do not know the meaning of several of the expressions used in it. Who, then, prepared the resolution, if it was not the Finance Minister or the minister-to-be from London ? I believe that what I am about to state is a fact, and that is that the resolution was prepared in its entirety by the Standard Oil Trust, and that the principles contained therein were dictated to the government by a representative of that trust. And I defy hon. gentlemen opposite to disprove that charge. The Standard have been operating in this country for about seven years. During that time the price of refined oil has gradually increased. Who can say that the price will not be increased when this storm blows over ? Who knows that the price is going to be continued as low as it is to-day. It was not the consumer in this case that agitated the question at this time. No ; it was the Standard Oil Trust, and the government could not stand the pressure. I do not find fault with American capital coming into our country and developing our industries. Far from it. But what I do find fault with is an American monopoly, whose policy is dictated from New York controlling the Canadian producers, the Canadian refiner and the *Canadian consumer, bleeding the people of this country for all they are worth and Mr. ARMSTRONG.
taking the profits to New York to pay out fat dividends to American holders of Standard stock. Why do not the Standard Trust, with their millions of capital develop onr industry ? They have spent some money in wiid-catting ; why do not they go at the development of this country's oil resources ? Oil has been found in many places throughout this country, and it would be most beneficial to the country if the Standard would spend money in developing some outside fields. The Leamington field has given us a new proposition. Formerly we thought the oil was only obtained at about 500 feet below the surface..
Will the hon. gentleman tell us where there was ever a well in the Leamington district at which oil was struck at 500 feet ?

I am sure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) misunderstood what I said. Let me repeat : I said that the Leamington field has given us a new proposition. Formerly, we thought the oil was only obtained 500 feet below the surface. But this field has several large producers at 1,100 feet, being a continuance of the Ohio strata. And these have been found w-ithin a few months. Why has not the Standard put money into the development of that field, I would ask the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) ?
I can tell my hon. friend that the development of that field has been by American money principally.
That is true ; but what encouragement will American capital have to continue in that business under present conditions ?

Is there a man in this House who believes that this change in the tariff will lead the Standard Oil Company to take an interest in the development of the oil industry in this country ? I do not believe that even the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) has sufficient faith in the Standard for that.
But I believe that this will raise the price of crude oil.

No, they will let the poor Canadian hunt around, and if he strikes anything real good and sure he will find the man from New York right alongside to divide up with him. We sit here and are asked to vote money for the de-

velopment of our mining industries, and, at the same time, we strike a blow at one of the greatest mining industries that we hare.
Let us look at the producing end of the business. Previous to the 7th instant, the producer and the independent refiner were masters of the situation. To-day the Standard has absolute control. The Ohio field is the nearest oil field to the Standard oil refinery. Consequently they will use no other oil. Tile price of crude oil in South Lima on the 6th instant was $1.08 ; loading on tank cars, 8 cents ; transportation to water-front, 5 cents ; cost of hauling to Sarnia, 10 cents-making a total cost at the Standard refinery at Sarnia of $1.31. Add to that the bounty of 11 cents per gallon or 524 per barrel, and you have a total cost of $1,831.
Those are not the market quotations at the water-front-$1.31 is not the price of North Lima oil at any waterfront point in Ontario.

I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) that these quotations have been investigated, and these statements have been made on the platform and in front of the Standard Oil Company's representatives, and they did not dare to deny them.
What are the prices today ? [DOT]
Does the hon. member mean to say that the- Ohio crude is better than the Canadian ?

Yes. The Canadian crude is 31 gravity on the average ? But North and South Lima oil average 38 to 40 gravity. And I will show the hon. gentleman iii a few minutes the difference between oil at 31 and oil at 38 to 40 gravity. It will surely be good news to the producer when he sits down to figure it out. Hon. gentlemen opposite will say that the price of crude is raised. Yes, but the Standard is paying on the price of Pennsylvania crude to-day, not on the price of Ohio crude. Will the Standard pay 29 cents per barrel more for a worse article, of a less gravity?
