Now, Mr. Speaker, the selling price of all these articles in 100 gallons of Canadian oil, amounts to $9.90. The selling price of all these articles I have referred to in the American oil amounts to $10.93, leaving a difference against the producers of oil in this country of about one cent a gallon. 100 gallons of Ohio crude is worth $1.03 more than is a like amount of Canadian crude. If you add the 25 cents per barrel less than the Standard may pay for Canadian crude oil to the 35 cents per barrel which is the extra value of Ohio crude over the Canadian crude, this gives the Standard trust 60 cents of a lever to hold over the head of the producers and independent refiners in this country, and encourages the Standard to the extent of 60 cents per barrel to use American crude, which in turn wipes out the bounty of 52 cents per barrel, and leaves the producer at a disadvantage of 8 cents per barrel with bounty added. Now, I wonder where you think the producers are with reference to that question. Tou will be told by hon. gentlemen opposite, who, no doubt obtain any information they require from the Standard] Oil Company, that the price paid the producers in Canada has been raised and lowered with the oil market of the United States for years. I wish to state,' Mr. Speaker, that that is not the fact. Pennsylvania crude regulates the 'price paid in the United States. A little over three years ago Canadian crude oil was selling at $1.75 per barrel, and Pennsylvania at $1.68, a difference of 7 cents in favour of Canadian crude. On the 6th of June, 1904, Canadian oil sold at $2.09 per barrel. On the same date Pennsylvania sold at $1.62 per barrel, a difference in favour of Canadian crude of 47 cents per barrel. Why this difference ? What brought it about ? Simply the fact that about two years ago an independent refinery was started, and producers had two buyers in the market ever since. This independent refinery has always paid from 2 cents to 3 cents per barrel more for crude than the Standard, hence we do not want to see it wiped out. What else do you do for the producer ? You restrict his market A number of producers, as I have mentioned, have been supplying gas companies, railroads and manufacturing companies with crude oil. That market is taken away. What else has been done to the producer ? He is held up to the gaze of everybody as a bounty-fed industry ? Can you conceive of anything that would damn an industry ^ in the eyes of our people more quickly than to call it a bounty-fed industry ? I imagine that 1 hear hon. gentlemen opposite, in about a year from now shouting on the hustings. Away with this bounty-fed industry ; it has no right to live, blot it out. The price of crude is controlled by the Standard, the value of crude is jeopardized, the market restricted, the bounty cry will help to kill us, and worst Mr. ARMSTRONG.
of all, and more humiliating than anything else, we are entirely given over to the Standard Oil Company, body, brains, boots and everything else. They place whatever restrictions they see fit on our oil. New York dictates, and we must obey. Talk about Canada for Canadians. The government of this country believes in giving up Canada for the Americans, Canada for the monopolists, Canada for the trusts and combines, Canada for the foreigners.
I have been asked the question several times. What is the price paid 1 Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite can tell something about that. Current gossip in the corridors says it is not less than $500,000, some say $1,000,000. You can depend upon it that when the Standard raises the price of oil one or two cents that amount will be collected from the people in a little over a year. Perhaps the Minister of Finance will explain why he made such a sweeping change when apparently no one outside the Standard Oil Company were asking for it. Not a deputation, so far as I can learn, has been to Ottawa asking for a change. It is only the Standard Oil Company that are asking for the tariff to be reduced. In face of the rising demand to assist other industries, and when the feeling of our people all over Canada is in favour of higher protection,'you single out one industry and deal it a blow that will cripple it for many years to come, if not retard its growth for all time. I believe I am justified in demanding of the Minister of Finance on behalf of my people, an explanation why this action is taken. Would it not have been better for the Finance Minister to wipe out this industry instead of encouraging capital to invest in it and then kill it by inches ? If you do blot out our business you drive thousands of the best of our people to foreign lands to assist in the development of their oil fields. Thousands of our people know no other business, and they will be obliged to seek other fields where they can find a like business. Mr. Speaker, our people are spending for the development of this industry hundreds of thousands of dollars every year, while, with a stroke of the pen, their lives, financially speaking, may be blotted out. What assurance have our people to-day that their industries will live and be protected for the next thirty days ?
If there ever was an industry, that needed a definite tariff policy, it is the oil industry. Let us look for a few moments at the independent refiner.
About two years ago a number of producers and retail men, being dissatisfied with the treatment they were receiving at the hands of the Standard Oil Company, built a refinery, in Petrolea. They have added to it. until they have a plant that cost them $250,000. Within the past few months they have enlarged the company, until they have among its stockholders, some 300 of the brightest and best men in Canada. They have purchased distributing stations in the

principal cities and towns in our Dominion, and are fighting the Standard all along the line. They had a deputation here a few days before the 7th, to wait on the Finance Minister begging of him to leave the duty alone. What did the Finance Minister mean when he said on page 4508 of ' Hansard
But there are two interests to be considered in the oil industry-the interests of the oil producer and the interest of the oil refiner.
I wonder if the hon. Minister of Finance had more than one refinery in his mind at that time. He must have known that there are only two refineries in this country and that one of these, the Standard Oil Company have been here begging and pleading to him to reduce the duty while the other company have been here begging and pleading to him to keep the duty on. He seems to have acceded to the wishes of the Standard Oil Company in that respect.
The Canadian capitalists can go. They can look for places to invest their money elsewhere. Did he think of Ithe Independent refiner then ? No, the Standard was on top and the poor Canadian refiner must suffer. There is only one independent refinery in Canada, and they came begging to the government, not to allow crude oil into our country at a reduction.
I wonder what these men think to-day. I wonder how they will like to take their orders from New York.
Up to the 7th of this month they were a free and independent company, bought crude oil in the open market, and owing to good business management were able to compete with the Standard Trust.
What is their position to day ? Do you expect them to build pipe lines to Toledo, build boats to bring the oil to Sarnia, build a pipe line from Sarnia to Petrolea, a distance of 17 miles, when they find that they have the Standard to fight in the American market for crude, and the Canadian market for refined, and by-products ?
No, there is not a man in this House would put a dollar into a venture of that kind.
Since coming into business, they have paid the producer from 2 to 3 cents per barrel more for their crude oil, than did the Standard.
Will the producer want to see them wiped out ? No, most emphatically, no.
You cannot expect any company with a working capital of a few hundred thousand dollars, to compete with another company with a few hundred millions, and especially when the larger company has thfe advantage, at every turn, and more especially with the Standard Oil Company with a reputation that is among the blackest on the pages of history.
The most profitable end of the refining is the by-products, and as every barrel of crude brought into our country, brings with it, all the by-products, the Standard will naturally have absolute control of that end
to the detriment of the independent refiner. Consequently the independent refiner, wherever he may be situated, in our country, is without a shadow of a doubt under the control of the Standard Oil Trust.
The Standard control the price of crude, and the price of refined in the United States. On the 7th of this month they were given absolute control of the crude and refined market in Canada, and having that, they control the price of all the by-products, and last but not the least they control the price the consumer will pay.
I have tried to prove to you that the producer and the independent refiner are in the hands of the Standard Trust. Now a few words with reference to the position of the consumer.
With the Standard Oil Company having fuli control over the price of crude, and the price of refined, and the by-products, where else can the consumer be but receive his price dictated from New York ? Does the farmer and workingman expect to get his oil cheaper? Time alone will tell that. It may be said cheaper to-day. He will eventually land where he has before when alleged attempts were made to help him by this government.
The history of the Standard Oil has been written several times, and any of you who wish to read, will learn, that the Standard have bought railroads, pipe lines, refineries, men councils, representatives in parliament, and dare I say governments ?
We will admit that the crude oil will come into this country, be manufactured and the by-products sold here. Let us see what that will do.
Take the Finance Minister's figures ; he says the consumption of refined oil in Canada is 25,755,450 gallons.
He says the saving to the people of 2\ cents per gallon on that quantity will amount to $643,886.
If the refined oil is all manufactured in Canada, as the Finance Minister states will be done, then there will not be any duty to collect, and instead of a saving it will be a loss.
Let us look at the true state of affairs. The government collected in duties on oil and its by-products in 1903, $885,945.44.
Now the crude coming in free brings with it the by-products, and the qualities that make refined oil. No refined is imported. Consequently the loss to the country in revenue is $885,945.44.
Add to that the bounty as estimated by the Finance Minister, $225,7S9, and we find a total loss of $1,111,734.44 to the revenue of this country and nothing gained.
This amount will be taken from the people in some other way by the government, but then the Standard Oil Company require it to help pay the 700 per cent dividend, to the New York stockholder s.
Tne petroleum industry has doue a great

deal towards increasing the revenue of this country.
Hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of pump tubing, gas pipe, lead pipe, casing-boiler plate, wire rope, iron and steel, and well supplies of different kinds, are imported each year on which duty is collected and these goods are used in the oil development, or if they were made in Canada would afford employment to Canadian workmen.
It is estimated that 1,000 cars of soft coal come into Petrolea alone, each year, practically all of which are used in the producing and manufacture of oil.
The Standard brings soft coal in at Sarnia by the boat load.
Why did not the Finance Minister take the duty off soft coal 7 I am sure that he could do nothing that could please the people of Ontario better. Why not take it off for mining purposes, if nothing else.
Tens of thousands of dollars are collected from the oil men each year as duty on the articles mentioned.
Would it not be following out the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, to have the coal and the articles we cannot purchase in Canada, such as casing, tubing of different kinds, wire rope, and many other articles, that we are compelled to buy and pay duty on, placed on the free list.
I want it to be distinctly understood that I am not in favour of a free trade policy. I am not a free trader. I do not believe in free trade as it is in England like hon. gentlemen opposite, or in reciprocity, or in annexation with the United States.
One of the Standard Oil Company arguments and one which will be used no doubt by hon. gentlemen opposite, is that the oil fields of Canada, are exhausted, and they have tested them and no new fields can be found. That statement was made by them months ago. Since that time the Leamington field has made great developments, and an entirely new field within ten miles of their refinery is being developed.
The fields being developed to-day, are as follows : The Petrolea field, Oil Springs, Bothwell, Dutton, Leamington, Pelee Island, Euphemia, Thamesville and Chatham. These are all producing fields.
Then there is large development work going on in New Brunswick, and the Northwest Territories, besides drilling rigs scattered throughout different parts of our country.
Remember that 12,000 people at least are directly interested in our industry, and every farmer in Essex, Kent, Lambton, Elgin and Middlesex would like to have his farm tested for oil.
Remember the oil business is a matter of labour, from beginning to end. Pumping rigs, drilling tools, boiler works, machine shops, refineries, well supplies of all kinds ; the handling of the oil, every move you make requires the labouring man, who with Mr. ARMSTRONG.
the farmer is the bone and sinue of this country.
No credit has apparently been given the oil business, for developing the gas fields of this country, and furnishing towns and villages with fuel and light. At Leamington the other day a well was struck that poured out as reported, gas at the rate of six million cubic feet per day. I wonder that more companies are not formed in different parts of our country to develop for oil or gas. The natural gas and petroleum report for 1S91 gives a number of places outside of the developed fields where oil has been found. It tells of oil being found near Collingwood, also in Wentworth county, in Barton township, in Oxford county, at Norwich, Ontario in Bruce and in the city of Ottawa. Who can tell but that gentlemen opposite while legislating here to injure the oil producers of this country are not sitting on top of rivers of oil. These are all outside of the tested oil fields, and if logs could be obtained of the dozens of wells drilled, much more interesting reports could be obtained. This report is thirteen years old. It looks like as if it had been kept in the cellar. Look at the oil development in the United States exporting $70,000,000 worth representing 1,070,000,000 gallons more than the home consumption. The total amount exported from Russia in American gallons, more than she consumed in 1902, was 422,488,925 gallons. I might tell you of Galicia, Austria-Hungary, Roumania, Germany, Itlay, Great Britain, New South Wales, New Zealand, Algeria, Persia, Dutch East Indies, Sumatia, Borneo, Java, Phillipine Islands, Hawaii, Korea, all of these countries produce petroleum many of them in very large quantities and here we are with a country big enough to bury half of them, and we are told by the Standard Oil Company that our oil fields are exhausted. \
War if constantly pursued by a nation is sure to destroy its trade and commerce, and very soon will bring it to bankruptcy, so with the oil industry. Constant tinkering with the tariff ; members of parliament for ever howling on the platform condemning it ; the press in many instances only too glad to get a slap at it ; a government with an unsetttled policy ; all this is enough to drive any industry to the wall, and discourage capital. Give the oil business a settled tariff ; give us a full report of our labours ; give us the encouragement of the press ; give us the support of the members of parliament for ten years, and I feel confident that we will not only supply our home market, but that Uncle Sam will have to raise his duty higher to keep us out. Not only that but we wTill bring millions of dollars into this country from foreign lands. On the other hand let the government, the press, and the people of this country keep on discouraging our industry, and it is bound to diminish our chances of success. I have great faith in the industry, but I have no faith in the hon. gentlemen opposite.

I imagine I see them on the hustings holding forth to their electors, with arms outstretched, and their voices at the highest pitch, telling the electors the wonders they have accomplished, in reducing the duty on refined oil, and placing crude oil on the free list. But then, Mr. Speaker, all the gentlemen opposite will not take that course, it would be quite out of keeping with the policy of the government of this country, if they were to follow one set of rules for the whole of Canada. They are a kind of go as you please party, with a policy for every riding. I can imagine I see the member for Brantford (Mr. Heyd) telling his constituents that they are all right, but what does his constituents say-I quote from the Toronto 'World ' of April 13, 1904 :

Brantford Board of Trade suspicious of Standard Oil.
Brantford, April 12.-(Special.)'-A strong resolution protesting against the reduction of the duty on crude oil from the United States was carried by the Board of Trade here tonight. A. K. Bunnell, city treasurer, in introducing the motion, stated that the movement for the duty reduction was being insti-uted by the Standard Oil Company under the pretext of making oil cheaper for Canadian consumers and incidentally giving employment to more men in their factory at Sarnia.
Mr. Bunnell further pointed out that the history of the company did not indicate that it would be advisable for them to enter the Canadian field more than at present. They would, he said, retard the future development of the Canadian oil fields and eventually increase the price of oil for the consumer.
A copy of the resolution will be forwarded to C. B. Heyd, M.P.
Then the member for West Lambton (Mr. T. G. Johnston) who assures you, that he has smooth sailing, and is perfectly satisfied with the result, had better listen to this little matter that happened in his own town. I quote from the Toronto ' Telegram ' the following :

Sarnia Trades Council will not declare itself on the question.
Sarnia, March 15-With Mayor Cook , and President Gedes, of the Board of Trade, and eight other representative citizens, President George Lambert, of the Sarnia Trades and Labour Council, was recently numbered on a committee to petition for reduction of the import duty on crude oil, as desired by the Standard refining interests here. Lambert was not present at the public meeting which appointed the committee and has been /unwilling to take an active part in the appointed work until he received the advice of his trade body, at the same time declining to sign the petition on behalf of the 800 men who constitute the council. It is now given out authoritatively that the Trades Council withhold any say in the matter of the duty reduction- neither supporting nor opposing it, and leaving their president to act as he sees fit individually. The labour men do not go into particulars in reporting their action to the public, but explain that inasmuch as the settlement of the question will affect every union organization in Canada as well as the Standard Oil Company, the wishes of the Trades Council at Sarnia-the Standard's Canadian headquarters-are better left unexpressed, however honest they might be.
The deputation will proceed to Ottawa as soon as Dr. Johnston, M.P., for West Lambton, intimates the time that the ministry is willing to go over the oil question.
I might also call the attention of the hon. gentleman from Brant to the 1 Courier ' of the 4th of March.
A very strong Conservative paper.
What about the Galt ' Reporter ' ?
I don't know.

Suffice it to say that all these newspapers condemn in the strongest terms any action being taken by the government in the direction indicated. The poor man's vote counts for as much as the vote of the manager of the Standard Oil Company, and these 800 men will see through the deal, aimed at ruining their Canadian co-workers in Petrolea, and elsewhere, and will resent the action of the member for West Lambton. But what about the hundreds of farmers in his townships, with oil wells on their farms ? I feel confident that when the farmers of those townships realize the position they have been placed in by this government, they will resent it, and resent it most emphatically. It will take more than standard talk and standard money to obtain their votes. How will they like to be bounty fed, when their market is practically wiped out by the Standard Oil Company ? How about the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) ? In what way will he vote ?
I have no complaint.

What will he say to the farmers in the new oil field which is to be of great value to our industry ? The Finance Minister could have read him petitions from that direction that would be instructive, asking the business to be left alone. Here is what the 'Wheatley Journal,' has to say :

Woodward, the well known oil expert and drilling contractor of Oil Springs, Ont., has been visiting the Wheatley and Leamington oil fields during the past few days and has pronounced the outlook one of the best for the largest producing oil fields in the Dominion. Mr. Woodward states that the depth of the wells, being four times that of wells in other Canadian fields, indicates long life to wells. The rock is all limestone, except the surface, with a light gravity'of oil and plenty of gas, which is a feature of the
[DOT]1851

best producing American fields. Mr. Woodward is a man of twenty-six years experience in the oil business in all its branches, and in hir judgment thinks that we have the largest oil fields in western Ontario, and from what he can learn, is of the opinion that if the tariff on crude oil is not removed during the present session of parliament it will not he asked for again for many a long year.
That is Mr. Woodward's opinion. That is not the 'Wheatley's Journal's' opinion.

Well, we will have to try and get something else to satisfy the hon. gentleman. Here is something :
Leamington, Ont., March 30.-Another oil gusher was struck here on Saturday when the Leamington Oil Company shot its No. 3 well. Thirty quarts of nitro glycerine were used for the shooting, starting 600,000 cubic feet of natural gas.
They say the gas is all played out up there.

Perhaps you brought some of it down to Ottawa.
On the same evening oil started to flow and on the following afternoon 80 barrels had flown into the company's tanks. The natural gas escaping from the well at present is estimated to be about 600,000 cubic feet a day, and the company is negotiating to supply the town of Leamington with gas.
I can imagine, Mr. Speaker, that these gentlemen are not anxious to have the duty on crude oil reduced. What about the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver)? I believe he is out of the House at present. I might refer to what the Montreal ' Herald ' of April 4, 1904, says :
Important oil strike.

Advices have been received in the Canadian Pacific Railway offices of an important oil strike in the Swift Current district, near Cranston, Alberta. It has been known for some time that oil existed there, but the first big strike was reported on March 22. The latest report is that a well has been sunk and an output of fifteen barrels a day is being secured.
I might also refer you to the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' with reference to that field. It stai'ts off thus in big letters :
Largest oil fields in America. Such will prove the Alberta petroleum districts. Former Winnipegger tells of richness of western fields.
I will not take time to read this, Mr. Speaker, but will hurry on. How will the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. A. T. Thompson) vote ? Let us see what comes from Dunnville :
There is cons4derable excitement here over the discovery of oil while a local company was drilling for natural gas, which abounds in this district. They struck a vein of crude oil at a depth of 800 feet on the farm of Joseph Boose, six miles from here. In six hours the flow produced a barrel of a fine grade of amber Mr. ARMSTRONG.
crude oil, which would be equivalent to four barrels a day.
I can imagine that the hon. member for Haldimand will be voting with the government on this occasion. I might also refer to the New Brunswick field, in which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) who is also absent from the House, is directly interested. I cannot believe that he will approve of this great injury being done to the oil industry of this country. I might continue, Mr. Speaker, but will only refer to one or two other members. One, the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) the only man in this country who claims to know the needs of the oil industry. I wonder if he is interested in this company. You would naturally expect a man that knows all about an industry to have some practical interest in that industry. I wonder if these men will approve of his action. The London ' Free Press ' says :
A London syndicate with a capital of $5,000 have leased for gas or oil purposes several farms south of St. Mary's, and will begin operations of boring for gas or oil at once.
I might also refer to the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes), who quotes from papers, and tries to get satisfaction out of them. He referred to Mr. Fairbanks, whom hon. gentlemen opposite will probably refer to frequently. All I. can say is that Mr. Fairbanks is a perfect gentleman in every way, an ex-Reform member of this House and is a crude oil producer. He sold to the Standard Oil Company the first refinery that they purchased in this country. He was one of the strongest advocates of the reduction of the duty to two cents per gallon, and has assisted the Standard Oil Company in every possible way. The hon. gentleman also refers to telegrams of congratulations which have been received, from Standard supporters no doubt. The hon. member would like to see a greater spirit of national independence-these are the words he used. Is he likely to obtain this through driving our industries out of existence ? Not one member opposite has given more than a passing remark with reference to the oil question. Most of them frankly admit that they do not know much about it; but when it comes to voting on the tariff, you will find them coming into their place, and when the First Minister cracks the whip they will all bob up serenely.
But then the ordinary Reformer looks upon the tariff as a measure to be treated in any way that may be to the advantage of the person discussing it.
I must mention an argument that I have heard advanced by an hon. member opposite. He came rushing to me as though he had found something, and said: Armstrong, I have a solution of the whole problem. Your people are all right. I said : How is

that ? The reply was :	Why, formerly
relined fixed the price of crude. Now crude fixes the price of refined. That was some days ago, and I haven't found the point yet. I imagine that remark must have had its origin with the man that knows all about the business.
Hon. gentlemen opposite don't seem to have the same fear of the Standard Oil Company as had Judge Lister, the late M.P. for West Lambton, who on June 20th, 1887, made these statements on the floor of the House :
I deny the statement of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Mitchell) that the foreign oil is better than the oil manufactured here. I say that the oil manufactured her'- is equal to any petroleum oil manufactured in the world. I frankly admit that in the past the oil was inferior, but the difficulties which the refiners encountered have been overcome, a.nd iwe are manufacturing to-day as fine a burning oil as can he produced in the world. In regard to the question of protection, every one understands the ground which I take upon that, and the ground which the party with which I am associated takes ; but I say that, if the protection to native industries is the policy of the government, it would be unfair to this immense and growing interest to do anything to cripple it at the present moment. We know perfectly well, as far as the United States are concerned, that the whole oil interest of the United States is practically controlled by the Standard Oil Company, and we know that they have been bringing oil into this country to sell at a less price than the cost of producing it, in order to get the control of this market. It would he against the interest of this large industry to do what my hon. friend suggests.
Is not 100 per cent enough?

100 per cent ? The moment you strangle that industry you will get the price put up at once. The people of Canada are today getting their oil much cheaper than they ever did before. If my hon. friend from the sea thinks he will he able to get it cheaper, perhaps he would for a time, hut the moment the Standard Oil Company came here, he would have to pay a higher price ; and to put the trade restrictions which my hon. friend proposes here would be to give them an advantage of al least 15 or 20 per cent more. So long as this is the policy of the government, that interest- the oil industry-ought to be protected and preserved against the United States as any other in the country. If free trade is to be the order of the day, that interest must go tfrith the rest, unable to exist without a high rate of duty ; but, if protection is to rule, that industry, which is a Canadian industry, a purely native one, an industry belonging peculiarly to Canada, should he -looked after as well as any others.
Also at 1148 of ' Hansard ' of the same year, he said :
So far as the manufacturers to-day are concerned, they are manufacturing an oil better than ever manufactured in Canada, and an oil equal in every respect in its burning qualities to that manufactured in the United States, and safer, so far as inflammable qualities are concerned, than any made in the States. The hon.
gentleman has told us that there is a duty of 100 or 120 per cent. I say there is no such duty at ail. The hon. gentleman will readily understand that the amount of the duty depends on the cost of the refined article. Sometimes it is 60 per cent, sometimes 50, sometimes 70 ; but, be that as it may, as far as this industry is concerned, under the previous administration this protection or duty, or whatever you may he pleased to call it, was put upon coal oil, and under that duty the industry has gone on and assumed the proportions it has attained to-day. And I may say to hon. gentleman that, in spite of the high protection which the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Mitchell) speaks about, the oil industry of Canada to-day is in a most depressed condition. Crude oil is worth less than 70 cents per barrel, and this is a lower price than has been reached, except on one occasion, in the whole history of the oil trade in this country, and refined oil is cheaper than it ever was before. I will not pretend to say that it is as cheap as it would be If there was no duty upon it at all. I do say, however, that, if you take off the duty, the Standard Refining Company have hut one object and that is to secure the Canadian market, one way or the other, and destroy the oil interests of Canada, and, if they succeed in doing that, the people of Canada would have to pay a much greater price for their oil than they are paying to-day. This is a large industry in this country ; it is an industry belonging exclusively to Canada, and if there is any industry which requires to be fostered in this country it is the oil industry.
Perhaps the Finance Minister thinks by bringing about this state of affairs he will raise a popular cry for hi's followers. They can say with extended chests : Look at what we have done-cut the tariff in two on coal oil, crude oil free, by-products reduced. Is there an election near ? And the Grand Trunk Pacific not quite ripe enough to pick.
Or is the government in a tight corner on the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme and wish to attract attention in a different direction ?	'
Canadians look at the refined oil selling for a lower price in the United States^, but do not take into consideration that the Americans sell by wine measure, while we have to sell by imperial measure, which is i more, for instance oil quoted on the other side at 12 cents per wine gallon, would c,ost at the same price 14h cents per imperial gallon. Instead of the American paying part of the tariff to get their crude oii, and the by-products into Canada as they did before, the Canadians pay the bounty now and louse the revenue. The manufacturer in this country will naturally ask, whose head will next come under the Reform free trade axe.
The government claim that by reducing the duty on oil, it will reduce the price to the consumer. Let us see how this policy has worked out in the past seven years, under hon. gentlemen opposite. I find the following figures in the Trade and Navigation Returns :

In the year 1897, the amount of binder twine imported into this country for home consumption, amounted to 3,364,840 pounds, valued at $180,190, plus duty of 10 per cent, $22,198, making a total of $202,388, which makes the price to the importer, with customs duty added, six cents per pound. The government made a promise to the farmers that by abolishing the duty, it would reduce the price to the consumer. Let us see how that was carried out.
In 1903 there was entered for home consumption :	Imported, 14,204,515 pounds,
valued at $1,810,238, which makes the price to the importer at the port of entry 12i cents per pound. You will observe that as the result of taking off the duty, the farmer has had to pay 64 cents a pound for his binder twine, an increase of one hundred per cent and a loss to the farmers of this country of $823,273.47. Then what about the hundreds of workmen who might be employed in manufacturing that binder twine in this country ? They are not taken into consideration by this government. And here our factories are shut down and our farmers are to-day in the hands of the binder twine trust of the United States, and paying twice as much for twine.
Let us look at barbed wire fencing imported for home consumption. In 1897 we imported 5,034,499 pounds, valued at $80,407, plus duty at 15 per cent, $12,506. Total, $92,973. This gives cost per pound of 1 8-10 cents to the importer. When barbed wire was duty free to the farmer, the government said : Surely you will get it at a great deal less price than before. Let us see how that works out. In 1903 we imported for home consumption 30,503,400 pounds. Just think of the number of men that would employ if manufactured in our own country. This amount was valued at $702,809, which, without duty, gives a valuation of 2 3-10 cents per pound, and proves to-day, that barbed wire fencing costs the farmers i a cent per pound more in 1903, without the duty, than it did in 1897, with a 15 per cent duty.
The loss to the farmers of our country is $152,517, and the increase in the cost of wire 28 per cent. We imported in 1897, 5,034,499 pounds, and in 1903 30,503,400 pounds. I wonder how many American workmen are engaged in the manufacture of these articles for us. It would be very interesting to have statistics to show the amount of money that has been paid out to workmen in the United States for the manufacture of these articles. This government reduced the duty on coal oil in 1897 and gave the Standard Oil Company the privilege of bringing in oil in tank ships :	Result, an
increased cost to the consumer of about 75 per cent. With the same flourish of trumpets, to catch the votes of consumers, they are making use of the same arguments with reference to the coal oil industry that they did with reference to the binder twine and Mr. ARMSTRONG.
barbed wire industry. Let us read, as a fitting climax of these arguments, what the hon. Minister of Finance has to say against trusts.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) allow me to ask him a question ? If I understand him, he is arguing that by taking off the duty, the price of the article in our market was enhanced. Would the same effect be produced with regard to crude oil by putting it on the free list ? Like causes, we are told, produce like effects.

Restricting the manufacturer and the producer in this country and turning over these industries to the trusts, what can you expect but to have these articles increased in price? I was about to quote the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on the subject of trusts.
It seems to be the inevitable result of high tariff policy that monopolies, trusts and combines will flourish. They may exist even in low tariff countries, but they could not possibly flourish under other conditions.
They have been able to flourish apparently under the low tariff policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. Think of the trusts and monopolies this government have created in the eight years they have been in power. The Standard Oil Company came into this country about the time this government assumed office. Perhaps the campaign fund was assisted then. Another election being not far off, further assistance is required and the people will continue to pay, pay, pay. Every man who votes for this resolution is a Standard man and will be so branded through out the Dominion. As representatives of this great Canada, we are sent here to do justice to all without fear or favour. Then, do not give away our industry to a foreign trust, and compel the producer, the consumer, and the independent refiner to receive their instructions from New York. The jubilee was a grand thing for us Canadians. It brought us nearer to Great Britain and made us better subjects. The Boer war, though it is to be deplored, yet brought us closer to the mother country. Our brothers and sons shed their blood that we might receive the protection of this mighty empire. The British preference will cement us still closer. We are all glad that we are British subjects, glad that we are living under the British flag. The greatest pride we have is that we are Canadian British subjects. Then, let us protect our country, protect our people, protect our industries so as to let foreigners know that they are welcome to come in and assist in developing our resources and to help to build up our industries; but, if their object is to tear down and destroy for the sake of filling their ccffers in foreign lands, then, we want none of them.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) who has just taken his seat does not expect me to go as fully as he has done into discussion of the oil question. Unfortunately, I am not as familiar as he is with that industry, and, if I undertake to discuss the question of the effect of the duties now, such action on my part might seem premature. In opening my remarks Mr. Speaker, I may say that it is with certain hesitation that I undertake to speak before this House in a language with which I am not very familiar. I know that when one speaks in a language that is not his mother tongue, he exposes himself to the danger of making very grave mistakes. And we find, Sir, in the political discussion of these latter days, that certain men and certain newspapers are not above taking advantage of mistakes of expression by those who are speaking in another language than their mother tongue, to cast upon them very serious reflection. Therefore, I say, I hesitate all the more in undertaking to speak in a language with which I am not very familiar. At the same time if, in the discussion of the questions which I shall touch upon to-day, I use some expressions improperly, I expect that there is fairness enough and sense of justice enough in this House to cause my mistakes to be overlooked.
My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) who has just taken his seat, tried to convince this House that the government was pledged to support the Standard Oil trust in the change of duties that have been submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I may tell the hon. gentleman at once that the government in undertaking to reduce the duties on refined and crude oil, has not acted at the instance of the Standard Oil Trust, but, on the contrary, had in view in the revision of the tariff the sole benefit of the people of this country. I am sorry that the hon. member has thought fit to cast a slur upon the government in this connection. Had he known what this government has done against the Standard Oil Trust on past occasions, even within late years, I am sure he would not have said what he did on that point. Does the hon. gentleman forget that, some years ago, w-hen the Standard Oil Company came to this country they made a combine agreement with the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific railway, by which their oil should be transported from Sarnia to Montreal at a less price than the oil imported from the United States by way of Niagara Falls to Montreal. That question was brought before the government. Complaint was formally made of discrimination on the part of these two railway companies ; and the government, after having investigated the question and given it full consideration decided to break down that combine agreement between the Standard Oil
Company's side and the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific Company's. In that instance, the government certainly showed that they were faithful servants of the people. Other instances could be given of the same kind. Let one suffice. Some years ago there was in Montreal an independent company engaged in the oil trade-the Gall-Schneider Oil Company. When this government introduced its measure under which oil might be imported into this country in tank vessels, this Independent Company petitioned the government for the right to use a piece of land in Montreal fronting on the Lachine canal. And the government, seeing that the granting of this privilege would contribute to make this company absolutely independent of the Standard Oil Trust, came once more to the rescue of the peopled, once more decided the question against the Standard Oil Trust and leased the piece of land required, thus making it possible for the Independent Company to bring in oil in tank vessels as the Standard Oil Company were doing.
Here is another instance, and now, because this government thinks fit to reduce the duty on coal oil, not for the benefit of the Standard Oil Company but in order that we may be delivered from the shackles of the Standard Oil Trust, this government is charged with being the friends of that trust. I am sorry, Sir, that the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Armstrong) has chosen to discuss this question in that light. In reference to the coal oil duty he seems to be able to see only two companies, the Canadian or Independent Refining Company, and the Standard Oil Company. The government is not acting in favour of either one of these companies, the government is acting solely with the interest of the people of this country in view. My hon. friend speaks of the Independent Refinery as not receiving from this government sufficient protection. The majority of the shares of this company are not owned by Canadians, they are mostly in the hands of Americans, and will my hon. friend tell me how much watered stock that independent company, which has in the last few years raised the price of oil in combination with the Standard, after having increased the price as they have done-will he tell me how much watered stock they have issued during these three years ? If I am correctly informed, and I know something about it, this company was formed three years ago. The next year after it was formed it paid a large dividend, in the second year it issued 40 per cent of watered stock ; and I am informed that not long ago it issued more stock, or those who had stock in that company took some stock in another company, at 100 per cent of what the stock cost those people. Now we see how independent these people are, and how they are working for the interests of our own citizens. We were

in the hands of these two companies and the government thought to reduce the duty-on coal oil in order to give our own people more protection and cheaper oil. The hon. gentleman says there was an understanding between the Standard Oil Company and this government because the very next day after the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech, there was a reduction on coal oil. I see by the papers that not only did the Standard Oil Company reduce their price, but the Gall-Schneider Company which is affiliated with that Independent Company has also reduced its price by the same amount ag the one by which the duty was reduced. Mr. Speaker, I assert that this step of the government has been taken exclusively for the benefit of our own people, and has already .inured to their benefit. I do not wish to discuss at greater length the coal oil question which has been discussed by my hon. friend from Lambton.
If you will permit me I will refer briefly to some of the subjects discussed last night by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson). In that speech the hon. gentleman spoke of the preference, and condemned in strong terms this government for having given a preference to Great Britain. I was much surprised to hear the hon. member for Lennox make that statement. Sir, in 1S97 this government thought it would be in the interest of this country to give a preference to Great Britain, and we alreadv witness the good effects of that policy in the fact that our trade with Great Britain has increased enormously. The policy of giving a preference to the English manufacturer in our market has induced the British consumer to buy more largely of our products.
Now, Sir, we are charged by some hon. members opposite with having reduced the British preference. The statement is absolutely incorrect, and I will prove it. If the hon. gentleman will look at all the facts he will see that so far from having reduced the preference, on the whole we have increased it. Take the woollen industry. On woollens there was a preference of 33J, but by the change in our tariff that preference is reduced to 14 28. On cordage the preference is reduced to 20 per cent. In these two instances only have we reduced the preference to a certain extent. But at the same time we have increased the preference on certain other classes of goods which are sent to this country, a reduction which will operate both for the benefit of Great Britain and for the benefit of Canada. Take china-ware, in which we have increased the preference to 50 per cent. On window glass we have increased it to 62-50 per cent; so that if we have reduced the preference on the two items I have mentioned, we have increased it on two other items. Taking the four items together, we find that the average preference amounts to 46 T9 per cent, or 13-46 per cent more than we had before.

In face of this fact how can hon. gentlemen assert that the government has reduced the preference?
Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lennox went on to say that we had increased taxation, because, as he says, the revenues have been larger. Well, Sir, it is possible to have a larger revenue without at the same time increasing the taxes levied upon the people. How is that to be done ? Under a very high tariff with absolutely no' imports, the revenues will be much less, because, instead of the articles being imported they are manufactured here ; and though the people pay more taxes, the money goes into the pockets of the manufacturers instead of into the public chest. But it is also possible to have larger revenues at the same time that you reduce the taxes levied upon the people. Let me prove that by this statement. In 1890 the average rate of duty levied upon imports our total imports was 21-21 per cent. The average rate of duty from 1896 to 1903, both inclusive, was as follows :
Per cent.
In 1896	 18-28
In 1897	 17-S7
In 1898	'. .. 16-95
In 1899	 16-70
In 1900	 15-98
In 1901	 16 06
In 1902	 15.99
In 1903	 15-87
So, Mr. Speaker, instead of having increased the taxes of the people we have virtually decreased them as I have just proven. We have been charged also by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) with having largely increased our expenditure. It has been shown by my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Bichard Cartwright) how this increase of expenditure has been brought about. But,
I may say that we have virtually not increased the expenditure in some respects because we are now charging less to the country for the collection of the revenues that go into the public chest than was charged under the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite. I think this is a fair criterion as to whether the government has been economical or lavish in its expenditure. I find by the reports, that in the Department of Customs in 1895-6, the last year of the Conservative regime, for every $100 that the Minister of Customs was receiving the country was expending $4.43 to collect that money. Now, as a result of the devotion to the public interest of a man like my hon. friend the minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) we find, that, instead of expending $4.43 to collect $100, we are simply spending $3.31 to collect $100 or a reduction of $1.12 per $100. I will not claim the same credit for myself but I will claim the same credit for the department which I have the honour to administer. In 1895-6, the last year of the Conservative

regime, for every $100 collected it cost tlie Inland Revenue Department $5. Now, we see that in tlie year 1902-3, instead of it costing $5 for each $100 collected, it only cost $3.50 and I expect that this year we will have a better showing still than that.
Has the hon. gentleman a less number now engaged and paid than in 1896 in connection with the Inland Revenue Department ?
I do not know whether my hon. friend has understood exactly the point that I have made.
Quite.

All that I wanted to prove was that when the hon. gentleman's friends were in power-I know he is not responsible for it because he was not then in this House-it took $5 to collect $100 while during the year 1903 it only took $3.50 to collect the same $100.
That is not the question I asked.
Whether we have a larger number of employees or whether we are spending a larger sum that shows all the same that we are very much more economical than his friends were.
Not a bit of it.

I think that cannot be disputed. I am sorry that a man of the intelligence and brilliancy of my hon. friend from Bothwell should dispute such a fact as that. If to collect $100 it costs to-day $3.50 and if some years ago it cost $5 to collect the same amount of money it seems to me a very simple proposition that this government is more economical than the other government was.
Now, the hon. member for Lennox stated that we had increased the debt considerably. It has been shown several times already that on account of the large sur<-pluses we have had in the last few years instead of increasing the debt it has virtually been decreased. But, the best way to ascertain whether the debt has increased or decreased is to take the debt per head. I suppose my hon. friend from Bothwell will not deny that the debt per head is very much less to-day than it was in 1895 and 1896.

The debt per head is, as the hon. minister has stated, less for two reasons. One is that the population has increased and the other is that we have been able to renew our loans at a lower rate than formerly.

Yes, but at the same time my hon. friend does not deny the fact that the debt has decreased. I am very glad to have that admission and it shows once more that I was perfectly right a few minutes ago in appealing to his intelligence
and briliancy to endorse what I was saying.
Now, coming to the question of the tariff,
I may say, that it has been charged against the administration of this government that we have an enormous balance of trade against us in our relations with the United States. It is true that apparently there is a balance of trade against us in our relations with the United States, but if we take the trouble to compare and examine the figures, we find that instead of having a balance of trade against us we have virtually a balance of trade in our favour. We imported last year for home consumption from the United States goods to the value of $128,790,237. We exported goods to the value of $71,209,969, leaving a balance apparently against us of $57,580,268. But we must admit that out of this $128,790,237, $60,000,000 worth represented goods which came into this country free and I suppo'se nobody would dispute the fact that these goods which come from the United States free are not imported for the benefit of the United States but are imported for the benefit of Canada* I will try to show by some figures how these importations were for the benefit of Canada. Take coal ; we imported more than $7,000,000 worth of coal. I suppose nobody will deny that it was for the benefit of this country. It is a well known fact that we have no hard coal in this country. We have to go to the United States and will anybody deny that it was for the benefit of this country that we imported that $7,000,000 worth of coal ? We have, therefore, imported free of duty goods to the value of $60,251,914, and deducting this from the total imports of $128,790,237, instead of having a balance of trade against us we have virtually a balance in our favour of $2,671,646. Let me put that in this way: The balance

of trade is apparently against us. We imported for home consumption last year $128,790,287. We exported $71,209,969, leaving a balance of $57,580,268. Of this $128,790,237 on exports $60,251,914 are on goods which came in here free. In deducting this iast sum from the above sum we reach a balance of $68,538,323, imports upon which duties are levied. Our exports being as above quoted, $71,209,969, our dutiable exports being $6S,-538,323, we have virtually a balance in our favour of $2,671,646.
It would certainly not be fair in establishing the balance of trade between Canada and the United States to ' mettre en ligne de compte ' raw material required for our markets or imports for the benefit of our farmers and producers.
Day after day the Conservative newspapers are calling upon us to adopt the same tariff against American goods as the Americans have against our goods. It has ben; stated time and again, both in this House and outside, and especially In the province of Quebec during these last two years, that It would be a great benefit to the farmers of Canada if we put the same duty on agricultural products coming from the United States as the United States duty on our products. I am here to assert, Mr. Speaker, that if we increase our customs duties on United States agricultural products, instead of it benefiting our farmers, it would expose them to retaliation which might prevent them from exporting any of their products to the United iStates. Take, for example, the commodity of hay. We imported from the United States last year hay to the value of $126,645. That seems to be quite a large amount, and the Conservative newspapers of Montreal frequently quote it, and say to the farmers : ' Look how you are treated, you produce large quantities of hay in your own fields, but at the same time the government allows this enormous quantity to come in from the United States.' Well, Mr. Speaker, when you look at the other side of the question it is not so alarming. The Conservative newspapers, while they give the figures for our imports of hay from the United States, always neglect to state that we exported last year to the United States hay to the value of $3,596,557. That is' not such a bad showing after all, then we can set off this $12§,000 worth of hay imported against the $3,500,000 worth that we exported. But there is also another side to the story which must not be lost sight of. 1 find that out of this $126,645 worth of hay imported to Canada not less than $121,000 was imported into the Yukon and British Columbia, while a very trifling quantity indeed was imported into the eastern provinces. In view of this, the charge so frequently made by the member for .faeques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that we are not sufficiently protecting our poor farmers on their production of hay, falls to the ground. I Mr. BRODEUR.
presume that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) does not contend that we can compete in the Yukon or in British Columbia with the Americans in the hay trade.
Since my hon. friend appeals to me, I would like him to explain what protection he is giving to the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are giving him a good market.
I don't know about that.

We are opening up new markets to our farmers for their agricultural products. That is what they require, and not high duties ; and there is no reason to grieve over this paltry importation of hay from the United States.
What new markets has my hon. friend given to the farmers ?

We have opened up in England a very extensive market for hay. Some years ago Canada was not exporting any hay to the English market, but now, owing to the policy of this government and the friendly trade relations we have established with the mother country, we are sending large quantities of hay to England. 1 desire to put on record a few figures in order to show how fallacious is the charge made every day against the government, that they are neglectful of the interests of the farmers in not putting a higher duty on agricultural products. In the item of live animals we imported last year from the United States $1,507,196 worth, and our total exports of live animals amounted to $14,455,576 worth.
To the United States ?

No ; the total export of live animals. Let me add that out of that $1,507,196 worth of live animals imported from the United States, there was imported into the Yukon, and British Columbia, and the Northwest Territories, and Manitoba, no less than $1,420,000 worth, there being imported into the eastern provinces only $87,000 worth. Now, in the item of barley we imported from the United States only $1,038, and we exported $457,333 worth. I presume that the one thousand dollars' worth of barley which we imported cannot affect in any way the trade of the farmers of this country in barley. Of oats, we imported last year $70,651 worth, and we exported $2,632,886 worth. Of pease, we imported last year $17,617 worth, and we exported $1,056,266 worth.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would like to ask my hon. friend if that was exported to the United States for home consumption ? Have these been exported to the United States for home consumption, or did they merely go through the United States in bond ?

I am speaking not simply of the exports to the United States, but of the total exports, in order to show that our exports are so large that the paltry quantities of goods imported into this country cannot affect our farmers in any way. Of wheat we have imported $57,794 from the United States, and we have exported $29,088,781 ;[DOT] and yet my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier says the pool; farmers are very badly treated. Of beans we have imported from the United States $26,332, and we have exported $79,801. Our total imports of these grains have been '$173,432. Out of this we have imported into tne Northwest, Manitoba, British Columbia and the Yukon, $125,000 ; consequently we have imported into the eastern provinces only $48,000, while we have exported $33,315,067. Now, I will give the figures with regard to hay. We have imported $126,646. Of this, we have imported into the Northwest, British Columbia and the Yukon $121,665 ; so that our imports into the eastern provinces have been $4,981; and I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend from Jacques Carties that we have imported into the province of Quebec, to the great injury of our farmers, the large sum of $104.
As my hon. friend is referring to me, I would like to ask him if lie is in favour of greater protection for the market-gardeners ?

I think the market-gardeners are having as much protection as they want. They are pretty well satisfied with the tariff as it is to-day. If at certain seasons of the year, let us say from January to May, we import strawberries, I do not know how they can affect very much those who raise strawberries in the county of my hon. friend, because, if I am correctly informed, in that part of tlie season, they are not producing strawberries.
What about lettuce ?

I suppose my hon. friend will not seriously contend that the lettuce produced by the farmers of this country is subjected to very serious competition from outside. I am sure he will not say that, and I see, from the way he made the interruption, that he did not speak very seriously.
I do, very seriously.

I find that of apples we imported last year from the United States $79,830, and we exported $2,759,047. Of butter we imported $131,745, of which there was imported into the Northwest, British Columbia and the Yukon $116,000, and into the eastern provinces only $15,000, while against that we exported $6,958,906. Of cheese we imported from the
United States $30,401, of which there was used in the west $17,400 and in the eastern provinces $13,000, while we exported $24,776,406. Of eggs our imports from the United States were $121,563, of which there was imported into the Northwest, British Columbia and the Yukon $120,000, leaving only $1,000 for the eastern provinces, while we exported $1,441,254. Now, the total provisions, including meats, which we imported from the United States were $1,774,896. of which there has been imported into the Northwest, British Columbia and the Yukon about $750,000, and into the eastern provinces about $1,230,000 while we have exported $50,569,442. These figures prove conclusively that the charge which has been made for some time in the press of the province of Quebec, that this government was not protecting the farmers of this country, but was permitting imports from the United States, is fallacious and cannot be sustained for one moment. And 1 may add that if to-day we see some of these agricultural products imported into the Yukon, whose fault is it ? It is the fault of hon. gentlemen opposite, who, when they uad the opportunity of having railway connection with that country and giving the farmers of the east a chance to send their products there, objected to the construction of that railway. Consequently they are guilty of everything that has happened as a result of their action.
