When you left tlie Chair, Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, X was trying to establish-and I think I succeeded in doing so-that the raising of the tariff on agricultural products coming from the States would not in any way benefit our farmers. I showed that our imports of agricultural products were much lower than our exports, and that therefore the prices of our agricultural products could not be in any way affected by the imports from the United States. I think I have shown also that the imports from the United States cannot in any way affect the agricultural products of the eastern provinces, because these imports are sent into the Yukon or British Columbia, and consequently the imposition of higher duties on them would not put our eastern farmers in any better position, because it would not enable them to export their products with any profit to those distant countries. I think I have clearly established that our country is to-day more prosperous than the great republic to the south of us. We have an abundance of wealth, our farmers, our labourers, our industrial men are in a prosperous condition. Is that the case to the south ? No, on the contrary, all the industrial classes there, are in a very depressed condition. I have in my hand a statement showing that for some months, instead of giving employment to the same number of labourers as formerly, a number of companies have been obliged to dismiss thousands of their employees and reduce the salaries of many others. Here, on the contrary, every one who wants to work can get something ; every one can earn money and live in comfort. But in the American republic the conditions are different. I see by the Montreal ' Gazette '-and I suppose no hon. gentleman opposite will question the authority of that newspaper- that according to the annual report published in April last of. the New York State Board of Mediation and Arbitration, there were more strikes in the United States last year than ever before. The strikes in the building trade alone during the summer in New York State caused a loss in wages of $6,754,751. I And also in the Montreal ' Gazette ' the following statement:
Susquehanna, Pa., June 12.-The Brie Railway Company has discharged 10 per cent of its working force, or 108 men, from its shops in this place. Like discharges were made in all shops on the system. This is the second discharge of 10 per cent within 30 days. The company is reducing expenses in all directions.
There is another example of the crisis which exists in the United States. And I may ask my hon. friends opposite whether they can point to any similar example in this country to that which I quote from the Montreal ' Gazette.' On the contrary I find Mr. BRODEUR.
evidence in the newspapers of the same date that there is a growing demand for workmen in this country. For example ' I/In-dustriel,' of Shawinigan, publishes an advertisement asking for a hundred men at from $1.50 to $1.25 per day. So we find, on the same day a statement in a prominent Conservative newspaper in Quebec that, in the United States, the railways are discharging their employees, and advertisements in the trade papers of this country asking for employees. So, the demand, from our friends on the other side for a tariff similar to that of the United States is not a reasonable one. I have much faith in their good sense and in their devotion to the best interests of the country, but I suppose they must be convinced, as I am, that it would be useless for us to try to copy the Americans in our tariff policy. It is better for us to maintain a system in accordance with our own conditions, not with a view to copying the United States, but with a view to promoting the growth and development of Canada. I read, only the other day, that in Fall River, in one day in April last, 10,000 people were discharged from the factories in that city because there was no more work to give them. I find also a statement with regard to the condition of employment under the steel trust. The number of workmen employed under the trust last year was 350,000, whose salaries amounted to $225,000,000. Through discharge of men and reduction of wages, the payments of accounts of salaries have been reduced by $60,000,000 since last year. We find also that, on the Southern Railway they have reduced the number of men employed by 3,000 ; on the Gould system by 7,500 ; on the Harriman lines, 8,000 ; on the Western lines, 10,000 ; on the Vanderbilt lines, 12,000; on the Pennsylvania system, 13,000 ; on lines running into Chicago, 20,000 ; and on lines of minor importance, 2,000. These figures indicate that Canada to-day is in a very much more prosperous condition than the United States. So, I am sorry that our friends on the other side are trying to induce this country to accept a fiscal system that has been so detrimental to the interests of the country to the south of us.
Now I see that my hon. friend from Pic-tou (Mr. Bell) declared the other day that the policy of the government should be to reduce the duties on sugar and tobacco. These are his words which I quote from page 4527 of ' Hansard :'
Why is it necessary that they should have surpluses to hoast of-surpluses of from $14,000,000 to $16,000,000 ? They could get clear of a large portion by extending the reduction of duties from molasses to sugar. They could also make a reduction in the duty on tobacco, which would prove an immense boon to almost every man who contributes to taxation.
I have every reason to believe that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) has the sympathy of those on his side in this and

so we must take this utterance of the hon. gentleman as a declaration of policy from the other side in favour of removing the duties on sugar and tobacco. I am sure hon. gentlemen have not given to this question the consideration that it deserves when they ask that duties which have done so much to build up the tobacco industry should be removed or decreased. When this government came into power in 1896, it is true, a movement had been begun among the tobacco growers in Quebec and Ontario in favour of an increase in the duty on tobacco. Several delegations came here and asked for this increase of duty as a protection to the tobacco growers. But the government of that day seemed to be much more inclined to protect other industries, and refused absolutely to protect the important industry of tobacco growing. I confess that when this government increased the duty on tobacco, we did not expect such favourable results as those we see to-day in the increase of the industry. And I am here to assert that, in spite of the increase of 10 cents on raw leaf, tobacco is selling to the consumers to-day at a lower price than before. I find by the reports of the department that in 1895-96 the number of tobacco factories of foreign leaf was 27, while only 10 were engaged in the manufacture of domestic leaf. At the end of last year the number of factories engaged on foreign leaf had fallen from 27 to 23, but on the other hand, the number of domestic and mixed tobacco had increased from 10 to 30. And that is the result in the number of pounds manufactured ?
In 1895-6, under the Conservative regime, we manufactured 9,609,184 pounds of foreign leaf tobacco, that is to say almost all the whole consumption was of foreign leaf tobacco. In fact we only manufactured and consumed in that year 474,205 pounds of Canadian tobacco. Now I am glad to inform our friends opposite that this policy has been so fruitful and has produced such good results that to-day, instead of consuming 9,000,000 pounds of foreign leaf tobacco, we manufactured last year 7,726,316 pounds ; and instead of consuming only 500,000 ponds of Canadian leaf, I am glad to announce to the House that last year we consumed nearly 5,000,000 pounds of Canadian leaf tobacco, or to be more exact, 4,921,181 pounds. So Canadian leaf has practically displaced foreign leaf, and that result, I claim, is entirely due to the progressive policy of this government.
Mr. MONK, I would like to ask the minister at this point if it is the intention of the government this year to reintroduce the law against contracts made by the American tobacco trust, which law was introduced last year and then dropped ?

That has nothing to do with the subject under discussion, but I may tell my hon. friend that the question 155
he has raised is now engaging my attention, and I expect that before long these exclusive contracts will entirely disappear. Well, at all events we claim that the policy of this government has displaced in this country the use of foreign leaf to the benefit of our farmers and Canadian manufacturers. While our hon. friends opposite were in power they were asked year after year to come to the rescue of the Canadian farmer; year after year they were petitioned to give the farmers a little of that protection which they were willing to give, so lavishly to other industries. They were willing to give protection to industries relying for their raw material on imports from the United States and other countries. Why did they not give some protection to those Canadian industries which relied on Canadian raw material ? Why did they compel those industries to rely on foreign raw material when we could have built up; industries relying on Canadian raw material ?

I would like to ask the minister a question. I notice among the tariff changes that the duty is increased on woollen goods that are made from imported materials and not increased on woollen goods that are made from Canadian wool. I would like to know how the minister can justify that distinction? He is arguing in one way and acting in another.

I am dealing with the question of tobacco just now ; I will be glad later on to take up the question to which my hon. friend has drawn my attention. But I may say that the point he tries to make in ho way invalidates my argument. I have proved that the policy of his friends when they were in power tended to refuse protection to Canadian farmers ; whereas we have to-day given protection to our Canadian farmers and have produced the results I have just pointed out. But that is not all. Not only have we come to the rescue of the Canadian farmer in that respect, but we have also done much for the Canadian consumer, as I will prove. I find by the figures which have been handed to me; that the consumer pays to-day less for his tobacco than he was paying in former years, that the fishermen of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are paying today less for their tobacco than they were paying before the change in the tariff. In 1895-6, the Canadian consumer was paying for the foreign plug chewing tobacco eighty-one cents a pound ; to-day he is paying for the same tobacco, a Canadian tobacco, just as good as that made from foreign leaf, if not better-he is paying to-day fifty-three cents a pound instead of eighty-one cents. For plug smoking tobacco he pays to-day fifty cents a pound whereas he was paying eighty cents under the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite. For cut smoking tobacco the Canadian consumer is paying to-day forty-six cents a pound, while under the



beneficial regime of hon. gentlemen opposite be was paying ninety-six cents or $1 for foreign leaf tobacco. So we find that in these three kinds of tobacco the consumer is paying to-day fifty, sixty and' sometimes seventy per cent less than he was paying under the Conservative regime. Not only have we succeeded in replacing foreign to-tacco by Canadian tobacco, but we are giving the consumer to-day a better tobacco and at a lesser price.
May I ask the hon. minister if he smokes ?
I do not smoke, but I do not think my hon. friend will dispute these figures. Will he undertake to dispute these figures ?
Most assuredly.

He cannot do it, because they are absolutely correct. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have shown that the policy of this government has been beneficial to the farmers, particularly during these latter years.

Before the hon. gentleman leaves that subject, I would like to ask him about the petition presented by the tobacco growers of the province of Quebec that the excise stamps should all be of the same colour, inasmuch as the green stamp does harm to the sale of the Canadian grown tobacco. What is going to be done about that petition ? Are we going to have stamps of a uniform colour ?

My hon. friend's question would draw me far away from the subject I am now discussing, nevertheless X may tell him that this complaint about stamps existed when his own friends were in power, and they were never able to mature any plan to remedy the evil. But I rriay say that I am now considering seriously this question and am having reports made by my officers, and I hope that before long I will be able to do something which will satisfy the tobacco growers of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish toi discuss much further the questions at issue in this debate. The issue between both parties is now well established. We have on one side persons asking for what I may call a trust tariff, and on the other side we have a government who desire to maintain a people's tariff. A trust tariff is against a people's tariff. Hon. gentlemen opposite want to establish trusts and combines in this country. We want, on the contrary, to have a tariff framed in the interest of the country, in the interest of the people, for the people alone and not for the trusts and combines. A tariff should be based not on theories but it should be framed with regard to practical exigencies and circumstances. That is the policy of this government in every instance, where we find that some legitimate indus-Mr. BRODETJR.
tries are suffering, these industries will be sure to get relief from this government. We are not going to create combines or trusts but what we want is to give fair aid and protection to legitimate industries. That is the policy of the Canadian government and we are willing to stand by that policy. I may say the tariff changes which were brought down some days ago have given entire satisfaction to the people of this country. Our hon. friends opposite are a little bit disheartened as a result of these changes in the tariff. We are glad to see that these changes ai'e meeting with the general approbation of the people. We are glad to see that men who at one time were not very friendly to this government are now willing to trust this government because of what we have done. We are satisfied with what we have done but our work is not finished and we will be glad to work to the end for the advantage of the people of this country.

'Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur), it seems to me in the latter part of his speech took a different ground in regard to the tariff from that which he took in the earlier part of his remarks. If I understood him correctly he explained to the House how that paying an extra duty on tobacco had not been the means of raising the price of tobacco to the consumers but that on the other hand the price of tobacco had been reduced. If I understood his remarks in the earlier part of his speech correctly I understood him to say that if the government put on extra duty on articles generally according to what we propose on this side of the House, the money would go in the hands of the manufacturers and the prices of these articles would be enhanced. It may suit the hon. gentleman to make that argument in regard to tobacco but surely the rule in regard to other things must work the same as it does in regard to tobacco. The present government, as I understood, had not increased the duties on farm products to any greater extent than those duties were when they came into power but they have, I think, reduced the duties somewhat on wheat and flour. The hon. gentleman referred in his opening remarks to the observations made by my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) in regard to the oil duties. I shall not detain the House by engaging in any lengthy discussion on that point because the ground has been so fully covered by my hon. friend from Lambton. However, there is one thing I would like to add and it is that it seems to me that the government have tremendous confidence in this great corporation known as the Standard Oil Company. If they realize their most sanguine expectations all right, but we know what the history of the Standard Oil Company is and while I do not want to have anything to say prejudical to any great corporation from my position in this House,

I wish to say that the Standard Oil Company's reputation for keeping agreements which they do not make in black and white is not the best in the United States and I would warn the government to be on their guard in regard to the promises which the Standard Oil Company have made them in connection with the reduction of the oil duty. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue used what I might term an elementary argument in regard to the cost of collecting the revenue of this country. I noticed that he brought a blush to the face of the hon. the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) when he referred to the tremendous economy which that hon. minister's department is displaying in collecting the revenues of this country. It seemed to me, I repeat, that this was a very elementary argument. It is the same argument that applies to most businesses where the output is increased and the running expenses on the percentage basis are less. If the revenue of this country jumped up a few millions of dollars it would take that much less on the percentage basis to collect it, the same as when a man's turnover in business runs up to a million dollars when it was only half a million before, his running expenses are so much less.
I was a little surprised that the hon. gentleman would use such an argument in this House. He also referred to the decrease in the debt and I propose a little later on to take up that question. I will not deal with that just now. He also referred to the question of our balance of trade with the United States and he demonstrated by the figures which he produced to the House that in reality there was no balance of trade in favour of the United States. I could not follow his argument very closely but I think that the figures which I shall produce later on will show that he was in error in respect to that question also. Then he referred to the question of hay. He mentioned the fact that we are now exporting to Great .Britain a considerable amount of hay and I understood him to say that it was because of our commercial policy with Great Britain which had been brought about by the present government and which was not in effect heretofore that this unexampled exportation of hay to Great Britain had been brought about. I fail to see how he works this out. I cannot see what these hon. gentlemen have done to make a commercial treaty with Great Britain, or to alter the conditions as they existed under the previous administration. If in return for the preference which they gave to Great Britain they had obtained a preference for our agricultural products I think his argument would have been well founded but as they did not succeed in getting any preference I cannot understand on what he bases that argument. It seems to me that the market gardeners' question was a rather delicate one for him and I take it for granted that 1554
in the magnificent and beautiful county of Kouville there are no market gardeners.
I think if there had been the hon. gentleman would not have dealt with that question which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) raised in reference to the tariff. But Sir, the hon. gentleman spent a good deal of time in discussing the question of hay. We all know that in that part of the province of Quebec which the hon. gentleman has the honour of representing in this House there has been in the past and there is to-day produced from the farms a tremendous amount of hay and that several years ago and further hack than that even the people in that part of the country sent their hay to the United States. The hon. gentleman, in discussing this matter, dealt with other agricultural products and he was trying to show that in regard to special articles of agriculture in regard to which we had a surplus production the balance of trade was not against this country and that hay was one of these articles. I am informed, and the hon. gentleman will correct me if the statements which I make are not absolutely right, that he, in years gone by, talked a good deal throughout the province of Quebec previous to and during election campaigns about what the members of the present administration, if they came into power, would do in regard to these agricultural products, not only in regard to hay, but in regard to eggs, grain, animals, and all those things which are the product of the farm and which were being exported to the United States.
When the Liberals were in opposition, they pledged themselves to make a treaty with the United States under which these articles would be admitted free of duty into that country and they held that by a mere stroke of the pen they could have accomplished this object. Well, the United States duty on hay was $2 a ton in these days, and when the Liberals came to power the Americans, to show there was no ill-feeling, raised that duty to $4 a ton. Notwithstanding all the coquetting of the Liberals with the authorities at Washington, the United States has raised up higher trade barriers against us, than ever before. The Minister of Inland Revenue told us that were it not for the Conservatives in the House of Commons and the Senate, the Yukon Railway would have been built, and we could now send Canadian products into the Yukon. I would like to have the minister elaborate this argument somewhat. I think he would fail in that. Yesterday in discussing the question of protection, the Prime Minister was rather severe on the opposition, and he made statements which to my mind were not warranted by the facts, the policy of protection was adopted by this country in 1878. It is no easy thing to administer a protective tariff in a country which previous to its adoption, had a policy of free trade, or a revenue tariff policy. The conditions in this country were peculiar at that time. We had only recently completed confederation ; the country was not so strong or so prosperous as it is to-day ; some of the provinces had come into confederation unwillingly it is said, and taking it all in all, the Conservative party had great difficulty in putting into force and carrying out the National Policy. In budget debates there are two questions which seem always to come to the front. These are the question of expenditure and the question of the tariff. I should like for a moment or two to deal with the question of expenditure, and I would like to discuss the statement which the Finance Minister made to this House regarding surpluses. In this connection I would put my hon. friend in the position of a president of a financial corporation. He is a man whose word in regard to the finances of the Dominion is taken all over this country. When he makes a statement people believe it to be true, and why should they doubt it ? When he tells us that he has so much revenue, that his expenditure is so much, and his surplus is so much, they take such statements as what the same terms would mean when used by the manager of a business corporation. My hon. friend said :
Our last session of parliament was so protracted that before the close we were able to have presented to the House the outlines of the condition of the finances of the Dominion for the year which had then recently closed, and since then the public accounts have been laid on the table, so that only a passing allusion is needed to the finances of the year which ended on the 30th June, 1903. I am not exactly sure what is meant by what is called the ' dumping ' clause in the budget speech. Our present law is rather elaborate; the Customs Act is composed of 254 sections ; forty-nine sections were amended m 1888, and year after year every clause almost has been dealt with in some way. We know that the laws of the United States are much more strict than our laws are ry ith regard to under valuation.
