The ' Globe, ' referring to an editorial in the New York ' Post,' stated that dumped goods did not have the mark of Cain upon them, and I thought that was a very apt allusion. Generally the conditions under which goods are dumped in another country, are, when there is an over production, or -when prices are demoralized, and if such conditions exist in the United States as have been stated by the Prime Minister, then this dumping clause will have no effect. If the manufacturer in the United States sells an article in his own country at a cut price, and if he sells it at the same cut price in Canada, then it cannot be said that he is dumping his goods here. It is my opinion that we should adopt the same system of valuation for duty as is in force in the United States, and then there will be no necessity for this dumping clause. The United States have few ports of entry, whereas we have ports of entry at various points throughout the different provinces, and we will need an expert at each port to tell whether goods are dumped or not. In Montreal and Toronto we require to have experts in prices of all kinds and these men have to be paid large salaries. How are the customs officers throughout the country going to tell the real price of the thousand and one kinds of merchandise that are brought in ? I believe it will be impossible to enforce this law, and I fear that the benefit will not result from it which the government seem to hope. We on this side of the House are in favour of putting an adequate duty on ail kinds of goods so as to protect our home industries, and if the government now in power would adopt that policy, they need not have to resort to all these complicated methods which they constantly seek to devise. The Minister of Finance raised the duties on wool-

lens and I congratulate him on that, but I fear that even now the protection is not sufficient to resuscitate the woollen industry in this country. However, half a loaf is better than no bread. I am glad that the government is returning to the principle of imposing specific duties, because I believe that without specific duties it will be impossible to develop and protect certain industries in this country. I am also glad that the Minister of Inland Revenue has helped the native tobacco industry by the duty which this government has imposed, if the result is as he claims. I am not objecting to these increases of duty ; I am merely pointing out what to my mind are the defects in the fiscal policy of the government. The Minister of Finance told us, that we were likely to have an inquiry into the whole tariff question, but it seems to me that if he were able to arrange the duties on coal oil and buggies and woollens without any investigation, there must be certain other industries which the government know require protection and as to which they did not require an investigation because the needs of these industries have been placed before them again and again by deputations which have come here to wait on the ministers. But some excuse had to be found for postponing the revision of the tariff this session. One year the excuse was given that the revision of the tariff was postponed because of the joint high commission ; another year the excuse was given that it was because the colonial conference was meeting ; another year, it was because of the agitation concerning our trade relations with Great Britain and the colonies, and so this year another excuse had to be found and we are promised an inquiry. I think, however, that I will be able to show from the remarks of the Finance Minister, that he is even yet a little hazy about this matter. This delay is working injury to a lot of our manufacturers. I am hot going to talk blue ruin ; but there are a considerable number of other industries which need assistance just as much as the woollen industry and the carriage industry ; and the problem* could be solved just as easily in those cases as in the others.
The Finance Minister said we might have to change the tariff because of changed conditions in other countries. I do not think that is the way to look at this question. We want a tariff that will be stable, one that will be suitable to this country in all conditions. The conditions in another country may be good or bad, but we do not want to raise or lower our tariff in order to meet ' those conditions we want a tariff that will meet all conditions. If it is all right when trade is poor, it will be all right when trade is better.
The Finance Minister said that the tariff was sufficiently good to induce manufacturers from the United States to settle in this country. I suppose he had in mind the Mr. KEMP.
American Locomotive Company, which has built a factory at Longue Point. I was talking to an officer of high standing in that company a few days ago, and I asked him what induced the company to come to Canada. He said :	' There is a good demand
for locomotives, and the duty on them is 35 per cent; and one reason which influenced them was that they claim they can do more business if located in a British colony with other British colonies than from the United States.' This man had travelled in Russia and in many other parts of the world, and he said that there was something in favour of an article that was made in a British colony. This is an argument in favour of mutual preferential trade between Great Britain and her colonies. In this connection I might point out that the great Westinghouse Electric Company settled in free trade England, and put up buildings on 160 acres of land a short time ago ; and we may well ask why it did that ?
We have been promised a tariff commission. What the Finance Minister said on that subject was this :
We desire to deal with certain things as they present themselves to us to-day we desire to deal with matters of urgency, reserving the question of a more general and more detailed tariff revision until an early date-
I would say hopefully next session, but at all events as soon as a proper inquiry can be made.
The Prime Minister said in regard to that :
Now, Sir, I have exposed the policy of the government upon this occasion. This is not, as has been stated, a regular revision of the tariff. That may come or it may not come, it will depend upon circumstances.
So that those are the remarks of the Finance Minister and of the Prime Minister, there is nothing very definite about the revision of the tariff. It may come or it may not come next session. Therefore, we are in the same position in regard to that as we were before. With us on this side of the House, protection is a constructive principle of politics, and the sooner hon. gentlemen opposite say what they mean by their tariff policy, as they did in regard to their policy of unrestricted reciprocity, the better for this country. We want to give a fair chance to Canadian workmen, Canadian brains and Canadian capital against foreign workmen and foreign capital. We want to say to foreign labour :	You are
protected at home in your own country ; hands off Canadian labour and Canadian capital. I believe it is the duty of this government to see in what way the industries of this country are being injured from time to time by the foreigner, and to say to him. hands off Canada. I do not think we ought to wait to revise the tariff until the chimneys are smokeless or until the win-downs are broken. The government pur-

sued that policy in regard to the cutlery industry in the constituency of my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd), also in regard to the woollen industry. I do not think we want a repetition of that sort of thing. The Finance Minister is not what may be called an enthusiastic protectionist; and it seems to me that in order to administer a protective tariff properly, we need a Finance Minister who is an enthusiast on the question of protection. The stock-in-trade of hon. gentlemen opposite is the prosperity of Canada-the tremendous revenues they are rolling up, and the big surpluses they are enabled to show as the result of this buoyant revenue. I think we might well ask the government, what acts are to their credit with which the pleasant occupation of spending money is not connected ? The spending of money is connected with a revision of the tariff. It might cause the government a lot of worry, but nothing to what the old administration had, when it put the protective tariff on the statute-book.
Before taking my seat, I would like to point out the amount of manufacturing done in this country. The Minister of Agriculture, for some reason, changed the mode of taking the census the last time from the mode followed previously, so that shows the condition of the industries somewhat differently. The industrial part of the census taken under this administration in 1901, I regret to say, is not published yet. I have been informed, in answer to a question on the order paper, that the figures are in the Printing Bureau, but we have not them at our disposal. I have the figures, however, and they show that according to the last census the output of the industrial establishments of this country was more than our total imports and exports. Our total exports and imports in 1903 were $467,664,685, and the output of our industries in one year, according to the census, was $481,053,385. I believe, however, that if the output of our industries were taken correctly, including all the products into which motive power enters, it would show that we are producing in our industrial establishments something nearer $750,000,000 annually. According to the census, the amount of capital invested in our industrial establishments was $446,916,487. And yet I heard one gentleman, who knew what he was talking about, say that he believed that three-fourths of the capital employed in our industries in this country was borrowed capital ; so that you would have to add to the sum I have named a tremendous amount. So that we have at stake in this country a tremendous amount of money, takingtogether the capital paid up and the capital borrowed, and it should be the duty of the government to watch carefully these industries. The wages paid amount to $102,984,668 annually. Then we have this tremendous growth of imports from the United States. It has often been pointed out by hon. gentlemen opposite that many of these imports consists of raw materials, but it is not of the imports of raw material that we complain. In 1896 we imported from the United States $29,101,646 worth of dutiable goods and in 1903 dutiable goods to the amount of $68,538,323. Our whole imports from that country are going up by leaps and bounds. I shall not refer to the question of the balance of trade against us in the United States, because that has been threshed out time and again, but I may mention that the balance of trade against this country from ail sources amounts to $10,410,000. This should not be. In the United States the condition is exactly the opposite. There the exports in 1903 amounted to $1,420,141,679 and the imports to $1,025,719,237, leaving a balance of trade in favour of the United States of $394,442,442. The excess of exports went in 1898 as high as $615,432,676.
Here is another illustration of our position. The imports of the United States in 1902 were $11.87 per head, while the imports for the same year in Canada amounted to $38.90 per head. Surely that is evidence of some weight regarding the amount of goods we are importing and the amount we are manufacturing. What we require is a protective policy suitable to the conditions of the country, and we do not want to be hewers of wood or drawers of water either for the United Sates or any other nation in the world.

I do not propose to follow the hon. gentleman through all his criticism of the budget nor is it my intention to call in question the receipts and expenditures or the methods used by the government in spending money. Ever since I have been able to follow the discussion of public affairs, I have found that the usual custom with all governments is to spend as much money as they can and that it is equally the custom of all the oppositions to find fault with such expenditure. The question I propose to consider to-night is simply that of the tariff ; and to my mind the budget brought down by the government this year is the most promising, intelligent and businesslike we have had since the late Sir John Macdonald introduced his protective policy in 1879. Like the budget of that year, the one brought down this year is inspired with the idea of helping Canadian trade and industry without any regard to outside circumstances, except in so far as they can affect Canadian business. That the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Kemp) and his colleagues on his side should criticise the budget is only natural ; and I shall only refer to their criticisms to show the weakness of the ground on which they stand. For instance my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Kemp) has just told us emphatically that the policy of the Conservative party is not to copy that of the United States on the tariff question. But the chief organ of that

party in the province of Quebec has been giving as the Tory platform-
What I did say was that we do not propose to copy the American tariff.
Exactly.
I think the hon. gentleman said the American policy.

X am glad my hon. friend has repeated what he has said, because what the Montreal ' Star ' has been urging the Conservative party to force this government to do is to adopt the American tariff in our statutes. Not only that ; but a former member of this government, the exMinister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) left the cabinet and joined to all practical purposes the Conservative party in order to force the Canadian government to adopt the American tariff. These hon. gentlemen have endorsed the attitude of the hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte). They have endorsed his speeches and his articles In his newspaper ' La Patrie,' in which every day during the past fifteen months we have had an appeal to the government to adopt the American tariff in order to produce the same results in this country as that tariff has produced in the United States. Well, I repeat that we are ready to take issue with the opposition on this point.
My position on the tariff question is well known. Even before some members of this government and before many members of the Liberal party had come to the conclusion that we needed protection, I declared most clearly and emphatically that I believed a system of moderate protection was required for this country. In the elections of 1890 and again in 1900, and every year since, in parliament, I have advocated a policy of moderate protection suited to the requirements of the trade and industry in Canada. On that ground I am still standing, as far apart from the present position of the Conservative party which is asking us to copy the policy of the United States as I was apart from the policy of the Liberal party when many of them wanted the government to copy the policy of England. What I desire is that we should not go outside our own borders to borrow a policy. What I desire is that we should not go to England or the United States for lessons in political economy ; or rather, there is one lesson we should learn from them, and it is that we should have a policy of our own, suited to our own needs. The budget of this year is the most comprehensive and sincere realization of that wish.
The hon. member (Mr. I4emp) disputes the fact that there has been depression in the United States under a high protective tariff ; but what have we heard for the two last years from Conservative speakers ? They have been preaching to us that we should raise our tariff in Canada because before long the depression in the United States will Mr. BOURASSA.
be such that a higher tariff will be the only way in which we can save our own industry. Only last year the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) urged the government to increase the duties on steel and iron because the condition of the steel and iron trade in the United States was coming to such a point of depression that it would be impossible for the steel industry in Canada to stand the competition. Sir, I think that the government have taken the only proper way to meet the danger of dumping from the United States and Germany. Certainly so far as the tariff of this year is concerned,
I hail it with the greatest satisfaction and congratulate the hon. the Minister of Finance on the means he has taken to prevent Canadian trade and industry from being interfered with by unfair competition from foreign countries on that ground.
1 cannot refrain from recalling my first address to this House on tariff questions-I think it was in 1898. On that occasion 1 caused a good deal of scandal amongst my hon. friends on this side by making exactly the same arguments that have been used this year by the Finance Minister as to the disadvantage to the Canadian consumer, resulting from dumping by foreign countries. I am glad that at last the government have opened their eyes to the danger and have adopted a policy which, on the one hand, does not commit us to the heresies of the Conservative party7 and cause us to fall into the excesses of high tariff, and thereby into the state of depression that exists in the United States-and yet, on the other hand, will protect Canadian industry against exceptional cheap prices, the only object of which is to destroy Canadian industry and leave us entirely at the mercy of the combines in the United States. Now, the hon. member says that there will be difficulty in exercising the power that we are asked to put into the hands of the hon. Minister of Customs. Un doubtedly there will be difficulty. There are difficulties in applying the present tariff. Every day attempts are made by the importers of this country to deceive the officials of the minister as to the value of the articles imported under the scale of duties now in force. But, Sir, merely because there are difficulties in the way, merely because there will be attempts to defraud the treasury of this country and to evade the obligations of the law, is that any reason why we should not adopt a suitable law and take the proper means to protect Canadian trade and Canadian industry against unfair competition V Should hon. gentlemen opposite come into power and adopt a high tariff, such as they say is required by Canadian trade, does the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. I-Cemp) believe for a moment that there will be no attempt on the part of importers to evade the duties Y The higher the tariff the greater the efforts that are made to evade the duties. Highly protected countries are always more subject than low tariff countries to attempts

to defraud the treasury and evade the customs duties. In adopting this proposed amendment, the government have taken a course which will make us an example to many other countries that are suffering from the same evil that we complain of. And, at the same time, it will be a warning to the manufacturers and traders of foreign countries and to their agents in Canada that we do not want to stand any more unfair competition.
As to the amendments that are made in the tariff this year, I do not intend to discuss them at great length. So far as the amendments proposed toy the Minister of Finance to the preferential trade system, I may say, without entering into details, that I am amply satisfied with them, not so much Decause of the particular effects of these amendments upon special industries, but because this is the first step taken by this government within the last five years to destroy the legend that has grown up in this country that the preferential tariff is something sacred, something that belongs to the shrine of imperialism, which cannot be touched, and which the government must not attempt to amend. The government have come back to the spirit in which that legislation was introduced in 1897, that is, that the preferential tariff was adopted for the benefit of the people of Canada, especially for the benefit of the consumers of Canada, and that it is to be dealt with by this parliament in the interests of the people of this country, as circumstances may require from year to year.
I admit that, from the declarations made by the Minister of Finance last year, we might have expected more changes in the preferential tariff than those which have been proposed by the government. In fact, Mr. Chamberlain himself told the people of England last fall that the Minister of Finance of Canada had virtually announced that he was going to repeal the preferential clause in case the British government and the British people were not prepared to meet us with equally favourable treatment. However, I entirely approve of the government for not having made more changes at the present time in the preferential tariff since they have made the announcement that a general revision of the tariff is to take place before long.
So far as the general revision is concerned, I may say that I am also fully satisfied with the broad lines that have been given by the Minister of Finance as to the principle upon which that revision is to take place. Hon. gentlemen on the other side have criticised the idea of appointing a commission to look into the details of that revision. I entirely differ from the opposition on that point -although I am sure I am far from believing, on general principles, in government by commission. Where questions of policy, of law or of constitutional principle, are concerned, I believe it is the duty of this parliament
to deal with them without invoking outside interference or help to prepare the work. But here is a question of business, which, with a lapse of time and the changes of industry and trade, is becoming more and more complicated every year. Here is the question of a tariff, any single item of which may cause disturbance in trade. For the moment you touch the tariff upon one item there is a reaction upon many other items which do not appear, at first sight, to be connected with it. Then there are the questions that arise between the different kinds of industry. For instance, steel, cotton and wool are the big industries that import most of their raw materials and turn out large quantities of products, and these become, in their turn, the raw material of some secondary industries, which, therefore, are directly affected the moment a change of tariff upon some products of the primary industries is proposed. /The question has become more and more complicated for us. i am sure that one of the difficulties the government had to contend with in receiving all those delegations from manufacturers was that one day they must have been asked to raise the duty on an article, and the next day some other manufacturer would urge a reduction of the same duty, because to increase the duty would be to raise the price of the raw material of some secondary industry and so, in effect, neutralize the protection given to it.
But there is one feature of the tariff question that is still more important to my mind and requires the preliminary work of a commission of experts before we deal with it, that is the question of our foreign relations as affected by the tariff. The influence of tariffs on trade relations between different countries has been increasing daily all over the world. Originally, all protective nations adopted tariffs for their own use and without regard to anything except their own industries and their own consumers ; right or wrong, it was a mere question of internal policy. But, by and by, as the interchanges of commodities between nations grew, and especially when large protective and manufacturing countries began to compete with Great Britain and to take away from Great Britain the supremacy which she held at one time in the matter of exchange between nations, the tariffs of the different countries have become more and more every day instruments of international relations.
The Prime Minister announced last year that he wanted to press upon the British government the necessity of granting to Canada the right to negotiate her own treaties. The government this year announces that when they next revise the tariff they are prepared to adojt the principle which has been adopted by Germany, by France and by several other protective countries, namely, the principle of a double-edged tariff, or a maximum and a minimum tariff. What does that mean ? It means

that we intend to begin a national life of our own so far as trade matters are concerned, and we wish to prepare for that by taking into our own hands the instruments wherewith we may meet foreign countries and deal with them as they deal with us, to apply to them a high tariff when they apply to us a high tariff, and apply to them a low tariff when they apply to us a low tariff. In other words, we want to deal with foreign countries on an equal footing. I cannot but applaud that idea. However, I must say that I take some exception to the definition which has been given by the Minister of Finance to that policy. He told us, if I remember aright, that the maximum tariff would apply to all countries that had a high tariff, although not discriminating against us ; that the minimum tariff would apply to the countries having a low tariff, although they gave us no special favour ; and that alongside of these tariffs, the preferential tariff would still apply to Great Britain and some of her colonies.
Well, Sir, I cannot see, if this is really the ground upon which the double, or I would say, the triple scale of tariff is going to be based, I cannot see how it is going to be worked out in accordance with what I understand to be the intention of the government. I do not see how their minimum tariff will stand as an offer for reciprocity to foreign countries so long as we retain the preferential tariff with Great Britain. Great Britain offers us no favour, she treats us just as she treats hostile countries, she offers us the same tariff that she offers the United States and Germany. At the same time I do not see how we are going to apply the maximum tariff to countries with a high tariff when we would have a minimum tariff to apply to foreign countries who have a low tariff, but who offer us no favours. The way the minimum and maximum tariff should apply is this :	The maximum tariff is to apply to
countries who refuse to make trade arrangements with us ; the minimum tariff wm be offered as an inducement to foreign countries who, having a high or a low tariff, would yet be willing to make a special arrangement with us and give us better treatment in compensation for the lower tariff we offered them. It seems to me, Sir, that we have altogether a false conception as to what is favourable treatment or harsh treatment in trade matters. The country that treats us harshly is not the country that has a high tariff and applies it to us in the same way' that it applies it to all countries ; the country that treats us favourably is not the country that offers us a low tariff, or even that offers us a free entry into its markets when it gives the . same privilege to all countries. Take for example the United States, with an average tariff of about 45 per cent. Supposing the United States were to offer us a pre-Mr. bourassa.
ference of 25 per cent off, while retaining a duty of 20 per cent against our goods ; would not the United States thereby offer us much better treatment than the treatment we at present receive from the British government who, while giving us free entry to her markets, also gives free entry to her competitors and our competitors ? who gives, for instance, no better treatment to us than she gives to Germany ?
The mistake we make is to introduce sentiment into the consideration of these trade questions. I well remember, even before I was a member of this House, when the Conservatives adopted the French treaty. The Conservative press and some members of the Conservative party, who at that time were not afraid of French domination, who at that time could derive no benefit from stirring up popular feeling in the province of Ontario against the province of Quebec-the Conservative press, I say, complained in the province of Quebec that some of the Liberals voted against the French treaty although that was the first treaty ever concluded by a Canadian government with the land of our origin. The position I took at that time was that in matters of trade I was first and foremost a Canadian, that if I were a member of the Canadian parliament I would grant no favours to France unless reciprocal favours were granted by France to Canada ; that my duty would be first of all to protect the interest of the Canadian people and to allow the people of France to look after their own interest. The position I took upon that question was exactly the same as the position I now take upon our trade relations with Great Britain. I say we shall not obtain any better treatment from the people of Great Britain, who are shrewd business men, so long as we show ourselves unable to deal with trade questions on them merits, so long as we say that because we are a British colony, because we are proud, and justly proud, of being a British colony, in matters of trade we are going to introduce an element of sentiment, we are going to make the people of Canada believe that while Great Britain treats us as she treats all the other countries in the world, we are bound to give her an advantage in our markets. I say the best way to obtain preferential trade with Great Britain is to show her that our people are as intelligent as they are. The best way to make trade arrangements with Great Britain, or with the United States, or any other country, is to show that we are prepared to stand upon our own bottom, ready to defend the interests of Canada first and foremost, without regard to the interests of any other country.
Now, Sir, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition thought fit yesterday to make a slight allusion to my opinions and some of my utterances upon that subject. He

said, in substance : How is it that gentlemen who were connected with the Anglo-American Commission, with a body endeavouring to get a treaty of reciprocity with the United States, and who were not afraid of the dangers which might arise from such a treaty with the United States, are now so much afraid of a treaty of reciprocity with England, and deprecate the idea of imperial preferential trade because they fear that it will endanger Canadian autonomy ? Sir, I am accustomed to being misquoted by Conservatives. I have been misquoted and misrepresented by many Conservative newspapers, and I am sorry to say that now, for the first time, I must put the leader of the opposition in the same Category. Sir, in all the speeches I have made in the province of Quebec against the adoption of Mr. Chamberlain's policy, I have stated most emphatically that I was desirous, and most desirous, of concluding a treaty of reciprocity with England. There is more : one of the articles of the programme of that very organization, La Ligue Natio-naliste, which caused so much scandal at the beginning of this session is that Canada should negotiate a treaty of reciprocity with England. But, what I have stated, what I state to-day and what I shall go on stating as! long as it is not acknowledged by this parliament and the people of Canada, is that in our trade relations with Great Britain we should stand on the same ground as we stand in regard to our trade relations with all other countries; that Canada is a self-governing country in trade matters, and that we should show the same spirit in dealing with Great Britain as we should show in dealing with other countries. AVhat I am most surprised at is that this should cause so much scandal in this country. Have hon. gentlemen opposite forgotten the events of twenty-five years ago when their leaders and their party, being taunted with disloyalty because by adopting the policy of protection they were discriminating against the mother country, they declared to the four corners of this land that if protection for Canadian industries was detrimental to British interests, so much the worse for British interests ? As to my hon. friends on this side of the House who have also, though to a less extent, become so tender on the question of the loyalty of Canada, even in trade matters, have they forgotten the day when they were advocating through the length and breadth of this land the policy of commercial union with the United States which certainly would have brought us very near the point of political union ? I was not at that time old enough to take part in the fights of the Liberal party and I do not know what stand I would have taken ; but I will reply here and now to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that I am in favour of concluding the best reciprocity treaty wih the United States the moment we can do so 156
without any sacrifice to our interests and dignity, and likewise X am ready at any time to negotiate the best reciprocity treaty with Great Britain and with any of the British colonies the moment that Great Britain is ready to treat us on equal terms, and to give us advantages similar to those which we give to her. Where is the disloyalty in that ? How can it cause a scandal ?
The policy that I have opposed for the last four years and that I am going to deal with now is not the proposition for a treaty of reciprocity between Great Britain and Canada, but it is the policy of Mr. Chamberlain. The policy of Mr. Chamberlain is as entirely different from the policy advocated either by the hon. Minister of Finance or by the hon. leader of the opposition as the American tariff is different from the Cobdenite free trade policy of England. The Minister of Finance told us that both parties in Canada were united in approval of Mr. Chamberlain's policy. He told us the same thing last year, though, I must say, I was glad to find that the tone was not exactly as tender and warm this year as it was last year. Last year the hon. Minister of Finance told us this :
It is recognized in England to-day that the line that Mr. Chamberlain is taking is the outcome of the policy of Canada, and therefore what Mr. Chamberlain is doing is precisely what we have been doing for seven years in the Dominion. . . . My sympathies are with the right hon. gentleman. . . . Our hearts go out to him.
It was a fervid declaration of love. This year naturally, after one year of honeymoon without much intimacy, the sentiment has grown a little cooler.
I think

Says the hon. gentleman :
I think I am justified in saying, and I think hon. gentlemen opposite will not find fault with me in saying, that practically the two great political parties in Canada are a unit to-day in favour of the principle of preferential trade. . . . Although there may be details in Mr. Chamberlain's plan which we are not called upon to deal with, and which we do not know to-day how we can deal with, inasmuch as he has practically taken up the Canadian policy, adopted it and recommended it to the British empire, to that extent we are heartily in accord with Mr. Chamberlain.
The bon. leader of the opposition has echoed these words. But it is rather interesting-and to my mind nothing is more illustrative of the fallacy of all this imperialism-to compare these expressions of Canadian sentiment with the declarations of Mr. Chamberlain. Speaking at Birmingham in November last, that distinguished statesman said :
We know as regards Canada that the Prime Minister of Canada, that the leader of the opposition, that Mr. Tarte, one of the most

toes such as those which in days gone by were prepared and signed by men who afterwards became their leaders and the highest representatives of Canadian loyalty.
What is Mr. Chamberlain's policy ? We have been told many a time, and even yesterday the hon. leader of the opposition told us, that Mr. Chamberlain's policy was but a reciprocity treaty between England and Canada. My hon. friend from St. Mary's division of Montreal (Mr. Tarte), whom I regret not to see in his seat, has told us in the province of Quebec many a time and his words have been echoed by several members of the Conservative party in that province-that the only issue that Mr. Chamberlain was proposing was to give us big favours for a very small return, that he was proposing to advance the price of our farm products, butter, cheese, hay, wheat, grain, cattle, meat, in fact all thei products of the farm, by granting a liberal preference, and that all he was asking in return was so small that it was not worth mentioning. On the other hand, Mr. Chamberlain declared at Glasgow, on the 6th day of October, that what the colonies were prepared to do was to give to England ' a substantial advantage ' in return for ' a very moderate preference.' What is that substantial advantage that Great Britain is going to obtain ? First of all-and that is the way Mr. Chamberlain, in his eloquent and forceful speeches, has always put the question before the working men of England-first of all, the working men of England will secure in the colonies a permanent market for their manufactured goods ; because, he says, the colonies are prepared to renounce the development of their industries so as to secure for British workmen and British trade a large and increasing market. What Mr. Chamberlain wants is, that the colonies should become a dumping ground for British products. There is not the slighest doubt about that, as I shall show. What Mr. Chamberlain wants further is to prevent the colonies from making trade arrangements with foreign countries. In order to do that he does not want to make a separate reciprocity treaty with any single colony. To that extent I would be entirely in favour of his policy: and as I have time and again said in the province of Quebee, I am ready to discuss on the part of Canada, as distinct from the other colonies, our trade relations and reciprocity with England. But Mr. Chamberlain does not want that. What he wants is to create an imperial tariff that will apply at the same time to Great Britain and to all the colonies, and which tariff will be prepared by an imperial council sitting in London, so that none of the colonies will be in a position to make trade arrangements with any foreign country. Is that the policy to	which both parties in Canada
are united ? Is the Minister of Finance ready to stand up here and say that

the Liberal party will renounce the right of taxation in this country ; and the right to make our trade arrangements with foreign countries ? Are the leader of the opposition and the member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp), ready to stand up here and say that they will stop the development of industries in Canada, so as to give employment to British labour ? If so, let them speak no longer of adequate protection for the Canadian manufacturer, the Canadian workman, the Canadian farmer.
But, further, Mr. Chamberlain wants to secure for Great Britain an abundant supply of cheap food-and, as he said himself at Glasgow-' another product of the empire, that is, men, '-men for the army and men for the navy ; because the workmen of England will not hear of conscription, and the British government being afraid of adopting conscription, they want to come to the colonies to take advantage of ' that splendid wave of imperial sentiment, ' and get from the colonies that which the people of Great Britain will not themselves give for their own defence. Is the Canadian government and is the Canadian opposition ready to stand up for that policy ? Why, Sir, we are advertising this country throughout Europe as a country in which the working man and the farmer may live in peace. The Minister of the Interior, in pursuance of his intelligent and progressive policy, has been for the last five years advertising Canada as a country of wealth and a country of peace. Are we going to invite the foreigner to come and live with us, and then are both parties in Canada going to join hands and say to Mr. Chamberlain :	' All
right, come and get the young men of Canada for the army and navy of the empire- take that splendid product of the empire, men,-and we will fill up their places with Doukhobors and Galicians.'
But, what is most amusing is, that that splendid advantage which is offered to us in the British market, reduces itself simply to a small preference on wheat. And even on this ground, Mr. Chamberlain takes good care to tell the people of Great Britain, that the moment the preferential tariff would have been adopted, the price of wheat would go up a little, but that soon after the price would go down, so that after a few years the price of wheat in England would be lower than before the adoption of a preferential tariff. I am told that the legislature of Manitoba has adopted a resolution in favour of the preference, because it thinks it is going to stimulate the cultivation of wheat in the west. Is it of good omen for the farmers of Manitoba, that three or four years after we have closed our bargain with Mr. Chamberlain, the price of wheat is going to be lower than it is to-day 1 That is the ground upon which Mr. Chamberlain has been standing for months back. He has proved to the people of England that so long as the registration duty on imported 156}
wheat was in force during the war, it was the foreigner who paid the tax. He has proved that the American transportation lines found a way to carry wheat cheaper, so that the price of wheat in England was not raised. He proved to the people of Great Britain, that when the wheat duty was increased in Germany in 1885, the price of wheat did not increase as fast in Germany as in Great Britain. He has proved, that when the wheat duty was increased in France, the price of wheat did not advance as fast as it advanced in England. He says that for the first years the foreigner will pay the duty, and that the imposition of the duty will have so stimulated the production of wheat, not only in Canada, but in Egypt and India, that the price of wheat will soon be lower in England. That is the very argument used by the Minister of Inland Revenue to-night with regard to the production of tobacco in Canada. Is it of good omen to the farmers of Manitoba and the great west, to know that after that bargain is concluded with Mr. Chamberlain, lands that are not now cultivated in India and in Egypt will produce wheat to such an extent, that the price of their wheat product will be lowered ?
Now, Sir, I promised the House that I would give a short quotation from Mr. Chamberlain, as to the effect of his policy upon Canadian industries. I cannot take it from this book which contains Mr. Chamberlain's orations for the past year, because Mr. Chamberlain was careful to strike out a few sentences from the revised edition, and so I must quote from the speech as reported in the London ' Times' the day after it was delivered. What did Mr. Chamberlain say as to the ' substantial advantage ' we are going to give to England for ' a small preference ? ' In the pamphlet which has been sent broadcast to the colonies, Mr. Chamberlain is made to say-and he is speaking from the bottom of his heart to the colonies :
After all, there are many things which you do not now make ; many things for which we have great capacity of production-leave them to us as you have left them hitherto Do not increase your tariff walls against us. Pull them down where they are unnecessary to the success of this policy to which you are committed.
I call the attention of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Kemp) and of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition to this, in connection with their proposal for adequate protection. When they criticise this government because the tariff' is too low, let them remember that Mr. Chamberlain is asking them to pull down the tariff walls further.
Do that because we are kinsmen-without injury to any important interest.
Mind the last words : ' without injury to any important interest' That is from the

colonial edition, but the English edition which appeared in the London ' Times ' read in this way :
Do that without regard to your important interest.
So long as Mr. Chamberlain was speaking to Canadians, through the ears of the good Scotchmen of Glasgow, he could say : never mind the imjjortant interests of Can-, ada ; but when the colonial edition was issued the words ' without regard ' were replaced by the words ' without injury.' Fortunately, I had more time than the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) to make these comparisons. Let us read further. Here again is the text in the book :
The colonies are prepared to meet us. In return for a very moderate preference they will give us a substantial advantage. They will give us, in the first place, I believe they will reserve to us much at any rate of the trade which we already enjoy.
In the genuine edition for Glasgow, London and a few other small places in England where people have a right to vote for the British parliament-that is, in the ' Times,'-the report reads :
I believe they will reserve to us the trade which we already enjoy.
Then he goes on, according to the book :
They will not-and I would not urge them for a moment to do so-they will not injure those of their industries which have already been created.
This is of course also in the report of the London ' Times ' ; but here is a short sentence! which I commend to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) who said the other day that we should develop and start as many new industries in Canada as possible. I also commend it to the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), who says that the policy of the Conservative party is to start as many industries as we can- to arrange the tariff so that it will bring less money into the public chest and will result in the erection of new' industries! What is the word of Mr. Chamberlain to these hon. gentlemen ? According to the report of the London 1 Times,' it is :
They will arrange for tariffs in future, _ In order not to start Industries in competition with those which are already in existence In the mother country.
That sentence disappeared from the pamphlet edition of the speech.
' Is that the policy of adequate protection to which the Conservative party is committed ? Is that the policy on which both parties in this country are united ? Is that the reciprocity treaty which the hon. leader of the opposition would like me to uphold ? Sir, I will apply to that policy a very able definition which has been given Mr. BOURASSA.
by Prof. Shortt, of Kingston, in w'hat, to my mind, is the most comprehensive discussion of that problem, both from an imperial and a purely Canadian point of view. Here is what he says :
What the imperial preferential advocates, on the two sides of the Atlantic, are trying to do is to divide an expected mutual benefit in such a fashion that each party shall receive about three-fourths of it, on the ground that the other must concede something extra ror the sake of sentiment.
I think this is the best definition that has been given of the imperialist policy. Butthnt is not the only advantage Mr. Chamberlain wants. He not only wants us to stop developing this country, to renounce our right, of which the Conservative party are so proud, of starting new industries in this country. Not only is Mr. Chamberlain asking us to renounce our right of becoming a self-sustaining nation in order to have the honour of supplying the empire with cheap food, and of becoming the dumping ground of the English manufacturer ; hut he has made up his mind that we are also to renounce some of our political liberties. I have been attacked for saying that if Canada adopted Mr. Chamberlain's policy Canada would lose a good deal of her autonomy. In the debate on the address, I quoted Mr. Chamberlain's speech at Glasgow, in which he said, in reply to Sir Edw'ard Grey, that the only means by which an imperial council could be created w'as by the adoption of that fiscal policy on which, according to the Minister of Finance and the leader of the opposition, both parties in Canada are united. He said that he started with the fiscal side of the question because the moment it was accepted by the colonies an imperial council would be forced upon them ; and at Birmingham he gave a definition of what that imperial council would be :
That imperial council, whenever it is established, will have to do with such delicate matters as Imperial defence, as imperial legislation, as imperial taxation.
Now, Sir, I will repeat what I have said in the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario. If the people of Canada have made up their minds that they are prepared to sacrifice a part of their legislative power to a small body of gentlemen sitting in London under the hand of the colonial secretary, they are free to do it. If the Canadian people have made up their minds to endow that small council sitting in London with the power of taxation over the people of Canada, let them have their will. If they have made up their minds to give to that small council the right to draw men from this country to supply an imperial army and navy, let them do it. But again I say, as long as the people of Canada are not acquainted with the consej-quences of that policy nobody in this House,

neither the Minister of Finance nor the leader of the opposition, is to say that both parties in this country are united on that policy, and no Canadian newspaper is to denounce as disloyal those who raise their voices against it. The first duty of Canadian statesmen, whether they approve of Mr. Chamberlain's policy or not, is to state frankly what Mr. Chamberlain's policy is- not what they want it to be, but what it will be if the people of Great Britain ratify it. I may be told that if Mr. Chamberlain's policy is what I have pointed it out to be, we are not obliged to accept it. Why then raise in this country hopes and expectations that cannot be fulfilled ? Why, then, keep the people on the other side of the ocean under a misapprehension as to the sentiment of this country ? We have had in the budget of this year, the most Canadian budget we have ever had, a declaration of fiscal independence on the part of this country. It declares that we are prepared to trade with foreign nations. It declares that we have adopted the preferential policy for the benefit of the people of Canada ; and so far as that is concerned, I greet it. But I say, do not tack on to it declarations of adherence to a policy the very opposite of the policy we are propounding. Bet not the opposition speak of adequate protection, of Canada for the Canadians, of the defence of Canadian industries, and at the same time profess attachment to a policy which would mean the destruction of Canadian industries, which would not mean Canada for the Canadians, but Canada as the dumping ground for the manufacturers of Manchester and Birmingham.
But, Sir, I may be asked, if the proposed policy of Mr. Chamberlain will be so unfavourable to the colonies, how is it that the people of Great Britain refuse to adopt it ? Well, one of the reasons may be that ' lack of imagination ' on the part of the people of the motherland of which Mr. Chamberlain complained so bitterly. I will not style it in that way. I will say that the common sense, the shrewdness, and the safeness of the people of Great Britain are what is saving her and us from the imperialistic mania-from that distasteful policy propounded by Mr. Chamberlain during the last few years, and unfortunately endorsed by some of the public men of Canada.
Then we should not forget, when considering these big advantages which Mr. Chamberlain is offering to the people of Great Britain in exchange for a small tax on food, that the people of Great Britain cannot afford to increase the price of their food today for any future advantage -which Mr. Chamberlain can offer. I have the authority of Mr. Chamberlain, as well as that of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, that one-third of the people of Great Britain are at present underfed-that 13,000,000 men, women and children in the British island have
not sufficient to eat every day. I have here the statement of Mr. Chamberlain endorsing that of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, to the effect that out of every seven workingmen in Great Britain now at the age of 25 who reach the age of 65, three will have to go to the workhouse. Is it surprising, therefore, that the people of Great Britain should refuse, even were they to derive great advantages within a few years, to have the price of their food increased to-day, when on that price depends the life or death of one-third of the population V But there is more than that. The people of Great Britain have not lost the sentiment of the balance of government. Happily for us, they know that the British empire^ has been built, both in commercial and military matters, upon the sound principle of decentralization, of the self-government and the Independence of tlie different parts of the empire. They know that the only way by which the empire can stand together is to have the legislative tie as slender as possible for the slenderer that tie will be the stronger will be the sentimental tie. It has been rightly stated in England that Mr. Chamberlain wanted to bribe the colonies. Bet me say here to the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp), and to all those hon. gentlemen who have sc often taxed me with disloyalty, that if their loyalty requires to be -bribed by the British government at the expense of the food of tlie British people, my loyalty and that of my compatriots, the French Canadians, is made of different stuff. We are loyal to the British flag and the British crown and British institutions, without being paid for our loyalty at the expense of the -lives of 13,000,000 of the British people. We do not want to be bribed, but at the same time we do not want to be deprived of any of our liberties , and I believe that I am expressing here, not only the sentiments of French Canadians, but the sentiment of the large majority of the population of Canada, if the policy of Mr. Chamberlain were exposed to them as it is in reality, and not as they suppose it to be. it mav be asked : But how is it, if Mr Chamberlain's scheme is so disadvantageous to the colonies, that the colonies appear to be so much in favour of it ? Well, that is easy to explain. Consider first the conspiracy of the press. Where is the llews-paper in Canada which has shown up to our people the policy of Mr. Chamberlain as it is shown up in England ? We hate a few weekly papers which have done so, hut not one of the large party papers has exposed this policy in its true aspect. WUat we have had is nothing but the sentimental and noisy arguments of the case-the sentiment of imperialism-and there is no worse bottom for making a good bargain than that of sentiment. My hon. friend from Toronto should not forget the rebuke that lie and some of bis colleagues were given at the last congress

of the Chambers of Commerce in England during the South African war, when an attempt to induce the Scotch and English members of that body to pass a resolution in favour of preferential trade was met with the protest of a good Scotchman, who stood up and said: Our colonial friends should understand that sentiment is one thing and business another. We have also the strange attitude of leaders of both parties, who are afraid to show up the policy of Mr. Chamberlain in its true light. I am happy to say in the presence of my hon. friend the Minister of the'Interior .(Mr. Sifton), that the first comprehensive declaration on the subject made by a leading statesman of this country was made by him when he showed the people of Canada, by his speed* at the Canadian Club last fall, what the consequences would be if Mr. Chamberlain's policy were adopted.
If hon. gentlemen want to know what mischief bogus sentiment can accomplish, let them go back to the time of the South African war. At one time if any one were to stand up in this country-not in England, because in England there is free speech-and say that the South African war was unjust, he wras exposed to be denounced for disloyalty. I have bad some experience in that line. The South African war was supposed to he a crusade for justice and equal rights, and it was most disloyal heresy to take the opposite view. But to-day, when the war is over, people are beginning to see through its hypocrisy, and we find now that the last word of that war is the introduction, under the British flag, of yellow slavery into that country ; and those who stood against that war have no reason to be ashamed of the stand they took, either as Canadians or British subjects. It is as a British subject, proud of my British citizenship, and as a Canadian devoted to Canada first and to Great Britain afterwards-devoted first to the country of my birth and the people whose interests I have been sent here to represent -it is as a Canadian and a British subject, desirous of remaining at peace with Great Britain and of seeing this country of ours develop and prosper rapidly, and become more and more every day the brightest jewel in the British crown-it is because I desire to see this country fulfil all the promises of its past and grow and prosper in that spirit of liberty w-itli which the very air we breathe is impregnated-that I have stood and will continue to stand as a determined opponent of Mr. Chamberlain's policy. What I have to say to the leader of the opposition on that question and, in a milder way, to the Minister of Finance

Mr. iSPROUEE. Hear, hear.

Yes ; because as far as that question is concerned, his deeds are better than his words. What I have to say is this. I think we should make it clear, both in England and here, that the Canadian Mr. BOURASSA.
people are ready to go a long way in order to have the best trade relations with Great Britain and make the best trade arrangement with the motherland and our sister colonies-and in doing that the government will find no more hearty supporter than myself- hut I think it is about time, to paraphrase the eloquent language of the First Minister, that upon this.as upon any other issue, we should look to the interests of Canada first and last.
1 hope this will be the last time I shall hear it said in this House that I am-an opponent of British connection or of good relations between Great Britain and Canada. I hope that it will be the last time at least when I .shall hear suc-h a charge from a gentleman of the standing of the hon. the leader of the opposition. The others I do not mind any more than I mind those newspapers which have taken up the habit of garbling words and of painting men under false colours, so as to gain a party success which they could not gain by discussing public affairs in a fair spirit and by describing men and their opinions as they are, and not as they would have them. As far as the people I represent are concerned, we are ready to make the best of arrangements with Great Britain, but at the same time we want it known that neither in political or military matters are we to consider any interests as superior to our own ; that the best service we can render to Great Britain, in our opinion, is to develop our country, to keep its population here, to bring in population from outside, especially from the United Kingdom. If Great Britain wants to have a strong foothold in America, she cannot gain it by closing our manufactures in order to give employment to the workmen of England ; but she can gain it by sending here the best of her sons to till our soil, and by sending capital to make use of our water-powers, instead of leaving it for Americans to come over here and Yankeefy this country. If Great Britain wants to keep the empire safe, she cannot do it by urging us to give our money towards the support of the British army and the British navy, nor by asking the people of the colonies to enroll themselves in the army and the navy. No ! On the contrary, she will keep the empire safe by maintaining a policy of peace and harmony with other nations and by allowing the colonies to develop themselves under the inspiration of the splendid principle of liberty which was introduced here with the British flag, and of which we French Canadians are as proud as any English speaking member of this House, or as the people of any constituency in Canada. Let the principle recognized be the principle of decentralization; let population grow ; let industries develop ; let Canada look to herself, New Zealand look to herself. Australia look to herself. Cape Colony look to herself. So will the empire be safer than by breaking up the old fabric that has stood so long the battle

and the storm, and won the admiration of the world, rather than by following the footsteps of the German empire or the Homan empire, which sacrificed the provinces, the weaker parts, for the benefit of the centre. The principle of decentralization is the bottom principle of the British empire, and Mr. Chamberlain should be plainly warned that the colonies will resist to the last his efforts to change the empire. While I am happy to support the budget of the government 1 hope that the time will come when the government will make the opinion of Canada known to Great Britain, and, as was said by the Prime Minister, let the Canadian policy be one to express the views of the Canadian people and for the maintenance and protection of Canadian interests.

I have listened attentively to the speech of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and was glad to learn from his opening remarks that there is at least one gentleman on that side who appreciates the benefit this country had derived from the tariff policy introduced by the late Sir John A. Macdonald and the Conservative party in 1878. The hon. member appears to be very favourably impressed with the proposition of the government to appoint a commission to consider the tariff. I am inclined to think that many other hon. members on that side are also favourably impressed with the proposition, and especially so in view of the general election, because they will now be able to go into high tariff districts and preach high tariff, and into low tariff districts and preach low tariff. The greater part of the hon. member's speech was what might be called a personal explanation of his views in reference to the tariff policy of Mr. Chamberlain. I shall not deal with that. I think that at this late hour, hon. members are not in the humour to listen to long speeches. I shall endeavour to condense my remarks as much as possible.
During the course of this debate much has been said in reference to the present prosperous condition of, the country. We on this side of the House are as proud of the present prosperity of the country as hon. gentlemen on the other side can be ; but it still remains for supporters of the government to show that the present prosperity is, to an important extent, due to any efforts of the present government, unless we give them credit for adopting the tariff policy which they strongly opposed when in opposition. We have had placed before us the diagram showing the increase in the exports of the country. I have looked up the items in the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I find that one of the principle items is wheat. In 1896 we exported 9,919,542 bushels of wheat. Last year 1903 we ex-poted 32,985,749 bushels. Here is an increase of no less than 23,000,000 bushels. What has the present government done to bring about the .present increase in wheat ?
Yery little that I am aware of. The Conservative party, under the leadership of the l(ite Sir John" Macdonald, secured the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway into our western country. The early settlers who went into that country were men of small means, and, for a time, there was no marked increase in the export of wheat But, in course of time, they went into wheat growing on a larger scale and their success encouraged men of capital to go into the business upon a scale larger still. The result was there has been a marked increase in recent years in the export of wheat. The following figures show the increase of our exports in the three important staples :

So that, in the three items that I have mentioned, we find a total increase of about $24,000,000. The increase in the lines that t have mentioned are largely due to the improved conditions of farming and also the bountiful harvest with which Providence has blessed us.
It seems to me that the government have taken a step in the right direction by increasing the minimum valuation upon horses imported. Put. to my mind they have not gone far enough to prevent altogetliei the importation of American scrub horses. Under the change they have made, the minimum duty on horses will be $10 per head, while the minimum duty on Canadian horses going into the American market is $30 per head. In 1903 there were several carloads of low grade horses brought from the western states into the county of Bruce. This would be of comparatively little disadvantage if they were used for work only, but the danger is they may be used for stock raising, and in that case there is danger from the inferior breed of horses. The horse breeders of Ontario have expended large amounts of money introducing from Great Britain the best breed of horses to be had, and it is very important that the strain of our horses should be kept up.
The government by their increase in the duty on woollens have shown that they have at last come to the conclusion that a little protection may be a good thing for a languishing industry.
I wish to say a word or two with reference to the furniture industry. During the present session I met a deputation of prominent furniture men who came here to interview the government. They told me that what they wanted was to have the same duty placed on American furniture coming into Canada as is now placed on Canadian furniture going into the United States. In western Ontario at the present time, there is a large amount of capital invested in establishments for the manufacture of furniture, which manufacture

appears to be a natural industry in this country. We have the raw material in the shape of timber, and the industry gives employment to a large number of persons and thus creates a home market for the products of the surrounding farm.
Where we find prosperous manufacturing industries we ought to find prosperous towns and villages. Where we find manufacturers prospering we find land values increasing. From the report of trade and commerce I find that we exported to the United States furniture in 1903 to the value of $14,754, while we imported furniture from the United States to the value of $518,217. Xu other words, we paid to the Americans $35 for furniture for every $1 that were received from them. And yet, Sir, this government refuses to grant to our furniture manufacturers the same degree of protection that the American people give to their furniture manufacturers. Speaking as a farmer, I wish to see not only our farmers protected but our manufacturing industries protected also. We are often told that the price of farm products is governed entirely by the British markets, I cannot agree with that statement. If that is so, how is it that land lying within twenty miles of the city of Toronto sells for $100 an acre, while an acre of land equally productive in the outlying districts only brings $45 per acre ? The British market is open to the products of both districts. To my mind the reason is because the land surrounding the city of Toronto finds a market for its products in that city, and the same principle applies throughout Canada.

I do not intend at this late hour to repeat to any extent the figures which were so ably presented by the hon. the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, and also by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. To my mind the budget speech should satisfy every man in Canada regardless of his politics if he has the interest of his country at heart. I agree with the Minister of Finance in his reference to one or two unfavourable conditions which existed during the past winter, owing to the severe weather, the heavy snowfalls and the late opening of navigation. But I think experience has shown that long winters with heavy snowfalls, although they delay the opening of navigation, have resulted in rich harvests for the farms, the fisheries and the forests.
I think it is admitted on all sides that Canada is prosperous to-day as it never was before. The Conservatives admit that fact, the only question is as to who is responsible for the wonderful increase in our prosperity. In the first place we are all willing to grant that Providence has had a great deal to do with the remarkable progress of Can- | ada, but we also claim that it is under the wise and judicious management of the I

Liberal party that these results have been attained. Time and again hon. gentlemen in the Conservative party have asked us to point out what the Liberals have done to bring about this wonderful progress. Well, Sir, if time permitted I could easily point out many things they have done. We know that the Minister of Agriculture, for instance, has done a great deal to increase the volume of our exports of cheese, butter and other' articles that come under his purview. Those of us who are engaged in business cannot fail to witness the great increase of our trade with Great Britain in those lines.
Now I wish to deal with some remarks of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) who undertook to reply to the Minister of Finance. He spoke in regard to the duty of kerosene oil, and stated that the Liberals ought to have taken that duty off years ago. I would like to know how that tallies with the remark of the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) who, in this House to-night, gave lengthy reasons why the duty should have been retained on kerosene oil. There are two distinct statements from the Conservative side that cannot be made to tally at all. So far as I am concerned, I shall be glad to go back to the people of my province and tell them that this government has reduced the duty on kerosene oil, because I know it will result in benefit to our people. The people in my riding were told in the last election campaign that when the Liberals came into power they promised to reduce the duty on kerosene oil, but instead of cutting it down by one-half they only reduced it by one cent a gallon. Now, I am glad to find that the government have seen tit, in the interest of the farmers and the labouring classes generally, as against a few rich manufacturers, to make a further reduction in the duty of kerosene oil. In other ways also I think this government have dealt, with questions affecting the public people in a way that is commendable. Although I do not think it is necessary to protect the woollen industries to any great extent, still I am glad that the government have granted some relief to some of those industries which, I am told since I came here, are suffering. At the same time I wish to say that I believe that if those depressed woollen industries had adopted modern methods and modern machinery they would have been able to hold their own as well as some other woollen manufacturers in Canada are doing to-day. I could name woollen mills that are prospering to-day and were quite satisfied with the tariff as it'stood before this last change. I have noticed that the Conservatives are greatly given to finding fault. If the duties are lowered they find fault. We are told to-day that taking the duty off binder twine had a bad effect. That question has been so fully dealt with thata- I am not going to enter

into it. X have also noticed that when the duty was slightly increased the Conservatives found fault also on that score. Tobacco has been mentioned time andj again, but I think the Minister of Inland Revenue has made a very satisfactory explanation in that regard this afternoon.
I need not take up the time of the House in talking about that at any further length. I notice that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) produced a table showing the increase in the exports of home products from 1896 to 1903. The increase in seven years was 3108,251,674 or $15,464,525 per year, and he claimed that that was not a satisfactory showing. But, let us look on the other side of the question. In 1878 the total value of domestic articles exported was $67,989,800. It increased in 1888 to $81,382,072 or an increase in ten years of $13,392,272, being $2,072,253 less than one year under the Liberals. In 1896 it had increased to $109,915,337, showing a total increase in 18 years under Conservative rule of $41,925,537, or an average increase per year of $2,329,193. The hon. member for Pictou also claimed that the Liberals are adopting the Conservative policy excepting the cautious financing of the Conservatives. I do not think it necessary to dwell at any length upon that point for the reason that that is also a question that has been fully dealt with. If the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte), had been in his seat when that hon. gentleman made his statement, I think he would have smiled as he had some experience as to bow the Conservatives managed the finances of the country in years gone by. The Liberals have so managed the affairs of this country that notwithstanding the fact that the expenditures have been increased in nearly all of the departments, we have yet to hear from the Conservatives in this House or in the country any great attack on the Liberals on account of then- expenditures. They know full well that any extra expenditure will be accounted for by the fact of there being greatly increased revenue. What are the conditions prevailing in Canada to-day ? There is full employment for willing hands at high wages. Our manufacturers are prospering as they never prospered before. Mortgages are being paid off as they never have been before and savings bank deposits have increased very largely. Has this prosperity which Canada is enjoying been worldwide ? The Conservatives have claimed that it has been world-wide, but my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) has very clearly pointed out that such is not the case. We have only to go to Germany, Russia, Australia and even the Lnited States to find that the measure of prosperity which Canada is enjoying has not been world-wide. I was very pleased indeed to hear the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that a commission would be appointed to
revise the tariff at an early day. I think this is a very practical way of dealing with the affairs of this country. I do not know that anything better could be done. As has been pointed out, the Conservatives some years ago, appointed a commission to deal with this matter which was not satisfactory, but I think we have already learned that the commissions appointed by the Liberals since they came into power, have produced good results, and I think we ought to feel quite satisfied that in the different provinces we can make some suggestions to the hon. Minister of Finance when the time comes, that will be valuable to him and beneficial to the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite would, no doubt, like us to adopt a policy of high protection, but they are not willing to grant that any changes should be made from time to time, claiming that the policy of high protection should be, like the laws of the Medes and Persians, unchangeable. I think that changed conditions require that the tariff should be modified or changed from time to time. Sir, a policy of moderate taxation and general good government such as the Liberals have adopted and which has increased the total volume of the trade of Canada from $230,000,000 in 1896 to $459,000,000 in 1903, should satisfy all true Canadians who place country before party. As has been pointed out by my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Canada of to-day is as far apart from the Canada of 1896 as the Canada of 1866 was from the Canada of 1896. I think that very aptly illustrates what has been done since the Liberals obtained power in 1896. Fault has also been found with the preferential tariff as arranged by the Liberal party. It has been claimed that it was not made absolutely perfect and that it did not anticipate every possible contingency from the outset, but hon. gentlemen opposite do not dare to question the advantage it has been to us in setting an example to the world. Several hon. gentlemen have already dealt somewhat fully with that question. I am only going to say that if nothing else ever came from that preferential tariff than the advantages we are experiencing to-day, I would consider that it had achieved very great results. Its advantages are well known to those who have had any experience in exporting to the markets of Great Britain. During the last three or four years, or since this preference has come into force, the products of this country have received a much greater share of attention in Great Britain than they ever did before. I have had a good deal of experience in shipping to the markets of Great Britain the products of this country, and I am proud to say that we have been able to reach a higher point for our cheese and butter than has been reached in almost any part of the world or by countries, at any rate, which have been shipping to the markets of Great Britain.
